The problem put in those terms, is a bit too stark in economic terms, and it is not the way I like to proceed in human terms.

Oral Questions
What developments caused the minister to adopt a position of stark choices, as he said in Sarnia on Friday that "the stark nature of the choice confronting us is only reinforced by the experience of the United Kingdom over the past year or so?" What caused the minister to turn 180 degrees?

subtopic: MINISTER'S VIEW OF RESTRICTIVE MONETARY POLICY AS OPTION TO CONSENSUS ON RESTRAINT IN VIEW OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I recall those words, and those words echoed similar statements I made in the November budget, when it became apparent in the third and particularly fourth quarters of 1974, and more so in the first quarter of 1975, that our cost performance was deteriorating as compared with the performance of our competitors. I said in Sarnia that the so-called traditional trade-off between unemployment and inflation might not be quite as apt, because if we do not get our costs under control-even in the event of a recovery in the United States-and if our cost ratios remain the same, we will not be able to penetrate that market nor even defend our own market; therefore one of the prerequisites to growing employment or the avoidance of massive unemployment in this country consists of bringing costs in this country into some sort of range which is comparable with that of the United States.

subtopic: MINISTER'S VIEW OF RESTRICTIVE MONETARY POLICY AS OPTION TO CONSENSUS ON RESTRAINT IN VIEW OF UNEMPLOYMENT

deflationary program of April 1971. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REASON FOR NOT PERMITTING MICHAEL PITFIELD TO APPEAR BEFORE COMMITTEE
speechtext: The practice is that ministers or members of parliament appear before committees and are supported by the proper officials. In this case, any questions related to the planning, orientation or administration of the office would be answered by a very senior official. The Secretary of the Cabinet himself has traditionally not appeared before parliamentary committees and this, I suggest, is for a constitutional reason-it is that cabinet discussions are privy to the cabinet. They are not subject to questioning in the House or outside. I believe it is for this reason that secretaries to the cabinet never have, as such, appeared before parliamentary committees, and since I am a traditionalist I am following the practice,

1.	With reference to the answer to Question No. 864, does the Minister of Finance intend to rely solely on discussions with provincial governments in order to attempt to regulate borrowing requirements for capital development purposes or is he considering any fiscal regulatory measures?
2.	By what means will the borrowing priorities of the provincial governments be rated and is the government intending to impose any controls on the inflow of foreign capital?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
1. The
purpose of the annual federal-provincial exchange of borrowing information described in the answer to question 864 is to aid the design and conduct of shorter-term economic stabilization policies through better data related to the provinces' role in the domestic demand for goods and services and the financing of the capital account of Canada's international balance of payments. The discussions have had a macro-economic setting, exclusively, and have not touched on the regulation of individual provinces' access to foreign bond markets. On February 27, 1975 the Minister of Finance announced the withdrawal of the foreign borrowing guidelines introduced by the government in 1970. Mr. Turner said the government no longer wishes Canadian borrowers to feel constrained by the request made by his predecessor and since repeated on several occasions to explore fully the availability of funds in Canadian capital market before floating issues outside of Canada. This specific request to Canadian borrowers is being withdrawn at this time because the current account of Canada's balance of payments is not now in a surplus position as it was when the request was made. Mr. Turner noted that the House of Commons approved an amendment to Clause 118 of Bill C-49. The effect of that amendment was to extend the exemption from withholding tax for interest on government bonds for a further three-year period-that is, government securities issued before 1979. This should resolve the immediate problem which has been of particular concern to the provinces-the problem of organizing their budgetary and borrowing requirements over the difficult next period of several years. The minister expressed confidence that these changes will help Canadian authorities and businesses in planning their financial affairs.
2.	The government has no intention of rating the borrowing priorities of provincial governments. The government is not contemplating imposing any controls on the inflow of foreign capital to provincial governments.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: UIC-NUMBER OF PEOPLE DENIED BENEFITS IN 1974
speechtext: The commission does not compile statistics on these component factors of "availability". To be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits, Section 25(a) of the act requires that the claimant be capable and available for work. The factors of transportation, residence, language competence and child care arrangements are but few of the multiplicity of factors which are taken into consideration in establishing a claimants "availability" for work. For example, distance and transportation are considered against the background of normal commuting practice of workers in the area in which they reside, the opportunities for return to suitable employment in immediate and contiguous areas, and claimants' duration of unemployment. The principle here is that the claimant who is genuinely interested in returning to work must be given a reasonable opportunity to make the adjustments necessitated by the realities of the labour market and associated conditions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. In accordance with Standing Order 54, I do now leave the chair in order that the House may go into committee of the whole.

The House resumed, from Monday, May 12, consideration in committee of the whole of certain items of the estimates for the year ending March 31, 1976, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Orders 58 and 59-Mrs. Morin in the chair.

Vote 1-Headquarters-Operating expenditures including reimbursement of the Ministry of Transport revolving fund in the amount of $200,000 for the value of stores which have become obsolete, unserviceable, lost or destroyed and authority to spend revenue received during the year, $18,467,000.

Madam Chairman, the minister had an interesting day yesterday as we started this experiment of marrying the old rules with the new. The minister, depart-
May 13, 1975

mental officials and members of the House were all trying to find out how parliamentarians can best scrutinize the expenditures of any department, not only the Department of Transport which the minister himself has said is a mess. This is a real problem for any ordinary member, but I know the minister is enjoying the experience.
The minister and I came to the House at the same time. He has always been on the government side, however, and has never had to worry about the scrutiny or accountability of estimates. While he is in many ways a great parliamentarian, perhaps he does not appreciate the frustrations of a member of the opposition with this kind of procedure. It was even worse when we were in committee for days at a time under the old rules and a minister and his officials had to remain until their estimates were passed.
When I came here in 1965, the total estimates of the federal government were $7.2 billion. When the rules changed in 1968 and the committee of supply disappeared to be replaced by the rather sterile procedure of opposition days and days for considering supply in the House, coincidentally perhaps, government spending seemed to run faster than Niagara Falls in the middle of spring: from $7.2 billion in 1965, spending increased to $28.2 billion in 1974. The increase in this year's budget over last year's is slightly more than $6 billion-almost the total amount of government spending in 1965, the year the minister and I first came to this House. I know this is not the minister's responsibility and that he is only responsible for the Department of Transport.
I hope that this experiment of having meaningful discussion with the minister on the floor of the House, in committee of the whole, will work out well. It could do away with the frustrations of members of the opposition who try to get answers to questions about the almost runaway government spending. I am glad we are trying this experiment; it should be an improvement over the old system where a minister sometimes had to stay in the House for a month before an item was passed because members of the opposition were perhaps given to rhetoric. I think this method is a compromise.
Madam Chairperson, Madam Chairlady-whatever you are-you are most courteous, and the most gracious ornament the chair has had. I say that because it is such a beautiful summer's day outside.
There are two points I want to make. I want to ask some pertinent questions about the Department of Transport and the dredging problems in this country. The second question is national in scope and has real interest for Atlantic Canada. I ask, what has happened to Atlantic transportation policy? In the words of the minister's predecessor, the Atlantic adjustment and freight assistance legislation was to be the first plank in an over-all, comprehensive Atlantic transportation policy. We heard those words when we last considered a legislative enactment dealing specifically with Atlantic transportation problems.
I wish to ask the minister two questions which involve the Department of Transport and dredging contracts in Canada. One has to tread a careful line here and not trespass on territory involved in court proceedings. There
Business of Supply
are certain areas which can be touched on; for instance, the problems of lack of supervision and control in dredging procedures, accounting procedures, and so on. These can be touched on without infringing upon matters under consideration by the courts.
My first question concerns discrepancies in dredging contracts. The reports of Auditors General for 12 years have referred to such discrepancies. I appreciate that Treasury Board, in a sense, has primary responsibility, and I know that many of these contracts are authorized by the Department of Transport and carried out by the Department of Public Works. The Department of Transport initiates requests for dredging. As I say, these matters were first raised in Auditors General reports.
My question is this: Has anybody's position in the department been changed; has anyone been fired or reprimanded because of problems to do with dredging contracts, overruns in contracts or lack of supervision? In other words, has anyone been held accountable, as it has been well documented in Auditors General reports for 12 years that there have been discrepancies and overruns in dredging contracts? Has internal disciplinary action been taken by the minister against anyone in the Department of Transport, or anyone in the Department of Public Work? Has anybody besides the minister taken responsibility for the improper supervision, or lack of supervision with regard to dredging contracts involving thousands, and sometimes millions of dollars of the Canadian taxpayer's money? That is the first question.
My second question is this: Have different procedures been implemented within the Department of Transport in the awarding of dredging contracts or their supervision? Again, I realize that the Department of Public Works is involved in this matter and many dredging contracts are initiated by the Department of Transport and carried out by the Department of Public Works; sometimes contracts are given to a subcontractor. Nevertheless, someone has jurisdiction or authority; that is obvious. Is anyone within the bureaucracy of the department to be held accountable? I do not want the minister to name anybody, but is there someone at whose feet this matter can be laid? Was anyone sloppy in administering dredging contracts? That is the gist of what I am driving at.
Therefore, my second question really is this: After this matter was brought to the government's attention through Auditors General reports, were changes made in procedure? Were dredging contracts awarded differently? Was there any change in the relationship between the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works with respect to the implementation of dredging contracts?
According to the doctrine of ministerial responsibility, the minister has over-all responsibility. Certainly, he shares that responsibility with others; that is the theory under which we operate. Obviously, the minister must take over-all responsibility. Can he say, without naming names, if anyone has been subjected to internal disciplinary action? Have changes in personnel been made, or have changes in procedure been adopted since this matter was first brought to the attention of the minister and his predecessors? As Auditors General have drawn attention to this matter for 12 years, I would be amazed to learn that efforts have not been made somewhere along the line to
5740

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
change procedures in an attempt to overcome discrepancies. I suggest that in the awarding of dredging contracts there has been at least sloppiness and, at most, negligence. I am staying away completely from any suggestion of criminality.
Let me give specific examples. Although they are not covered by these estimates, they show what can happen. One incident took place in 1963 concerning a development to do with the St. Maurice River. In that case, the Department of Transport asked the Department of Public Works to do some dredging work in the St. Maurice River in connection with the development of a municipal park and marina by the city of Trois-Rivieres. The Public Works Department stated that it would be prepared to recommend only the sharing of the cost of dredging the access channel, which would mean a financial outlay of about $9,000, but that it could accept no financial responsibility for the mooring basin and the berthing area associated with the municipal park. The department suggested that the city should negotiate a contract for the dredging and that the payment by the department would be in the form of a contribution to the city. In other words, the Department of Public Works said, "We can only do so much."
It had been a long-term policy of the Department of Public Works to limit its participation in the cost of dredging access channels from private areas to main channels to sharing the cost equally with those desiring such access, and not to accept any financial responsibility for dredging slips or berth areas considered to be of a private nature. That, at any rate, is what the department said to the city of Trois-Rivieres. But in January, 1963, Treasury Board gave the Department of Public Works $45,000 to cover the full cost of dredging not only the access channel but the berth and mooring areas.
I appreciate that the contract involved the Department of Public Works and Treasury Board, but I want to know whether the Department of Transport was involved in any way with the contract concerning the St. Maurice River at Trois-Rivieres. Originally, the department agreed on a contract costing $9,000, but in January, 1963, Treasury Board gave the Department of Public Works $45,000 to cover the full cost of dredging of the marina and berth areas.
I suggest that Treasury Board should never have given the Department of Public Works this money. That action was at variance with established policy. As well, it was open to question because there is a long-standing policy which says that financial assistance may be given to outside organizations only from parliamentary appropriations specifically provided or intended for such assistance. This was a payment which had never been approved by parliament. It was for dredging which was, obviously, of a private nature and which would enhance, in effect, a private operation.
In 1966, further interesting examples of dredging irregularities arose. These involved more directly the Department of Transport. A number of test borings for dredging work were made which proved to be inadequate. In at least four Auditors General reports, dredging or construction costs exceeded estimates because test borings produced results that did not accurately reflect the nature of the terrain to be dredged or excavated. Of course,

Treasury Board has the over-all supervision of the expenditure of money; it has the final responsibility. I must say I tried to bring this matter forward at the time Treasury Board estimates were on the floor of the House last Friday. However, because of a procedural hassle and other problems at that time, it was not possible to ask these questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am sorry but I must inform the hon. minister that the hon. member chose to speak for 15 minutes; his time has therefore expired. Perhaps the minister could take note of the questions and answer them this evening.
The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville.

Madam Chairman, I want to direct a few questions to the Minister of Transport. The part of the country I come from has for a long time benefited from the Crowsnest pass agreement of many, many years ago with regard to shipping grain. Recently there has been a bit of controversy in the prairies because of a series of telegrams sent to the Premier of Saskatchewan by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. Many statements have been made by the minister and other Liberal politicians in western Canada, including the Prime Minister, and a lot of farmers are worried that the present government will change the Crowsnest pass agreement which provides lower shipping costs for grain shipped by prairie farmers.
I want to ask the minister his position with regard to the Crowsnest pass agreement. What concerns me is that the Minister of Justice seems to be getting too involved in the responsibilities of the Minister of Transport. The Minister of Transport should be the one to decide whether there is to be a change in the agreement. What is the minister's position with regard to the Crowsnest pass agreement? Will he answer yes or no as to whether there will be a change in that agreement between now and the next election which will probably be some time in 1978?

Madam Chairman, I have stated in the House, and in the west, my position as far as the Crowsnest rates are concerned. The Crowsnest pass agreement, the Maritime Freight Rates Act, the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act and many other special measures exist to help one region or one product. This is part of the policy on which we are working. There is no doubt that the Crowsnest pass rate should be part of our national policy. However, in what form will it be? My only interest is the advantage it will give to the western farmers. I do not think they should have any worse deal under any future policy.
May 13, 1975

The Maritime Freight Rates Act was modified last year; in fact, it was improved: we increased the 30 per cent subsidy to 50 per cent for exports from the Atlantic provinces. I do not think anyone in the department or in the government thinks we should get rid of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. That does not mean that in the future, in co-operation with the Atlantic provinces, we will not find a better formula for helping industrialization or the export trade in that very important region of Canada.
I would like this to be clear. This is an advantage to the western farmers. If ever the policy is changed, the advantage should be no less than it is now. Whether this will be forever, I cannot say. I cannot say that no statute of Canada or even the constitution of Canada will never be changed. How could I say that? However, I can say that it is our intention to keep the advantages which the farmers in the west now receive.
Madam Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I ask the minister to correct himself. I think this needs correction. He said the Maritime Freight Rates Act-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville has the floor for the purpose of asking questions.

With respect, the minister is not very clear. He talked about the benefits of the Crowsnest agreement and the possibility of giving those benefits to the farmers in a different form. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board said the same thing in the House yesterday: he said he would like to see the benefits preserved but perhaps in a different way. The farmers are worried about what might be that different form. Can the minister give an absolute guarantee that the government will not tamper with the Crowsnest agreement between now and the next federal election? This is what the farmers in the prairie provinces are asking me.
I would like the minister to be a little more clear. Will he, or will he not, tamper with the Crowsnest agreement? He talks about a different form. To what kind of form is he referring? What kind of benefits is he talking about? I want to know definitely.

Madam Chairman, even if it seems the hon. member did not understand what I said, I know that he did understand. He wants me to say that Crowsnest is there and will remain there, without any change, forever.
Until 1978. At least until that time.

Chances are we would not have time to change it before then. If there is a change before 1978, which I doubt very much, it will keep the advantages and benefits the farmers now have. I sometimes go to the west. It is unfortunate the hon. member does not go more often. The farmers understand what I am saying. They do not care about the name; what they want is a guarantee that they will not have to pay more for the movement of grain. We want to keep this is in the same way as we have the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I expect a question later about that, and I am ready to answer it.

He's waffling.
Business of Supply

My hon. friend says the minister is waffling. I heard the minister say-this is what I am nervous about-that if there is any change, the farmers will still have the same benefits. Having him think that is not good enough. Can he guarantee there will be no change whatsoever which will be detrimental to the farmers, between now and the next election?
The only thing I can say, as Minister of Transport, as one who presided over the new policy which is going to be known, I hope, in a short while-
As the Marchand policy?

-is that at no moment did we discuss in our working group that the Crowsnest pass rates should be changed. We are going to work on freight rates; we are going to work in co-operation with the Atlantic provinces, but nobody is going to make me make a statement-and I hope this is clear-that something which is in the statutes of Canada is not going to be changed. I am not going to make any definite statement, because I do not have this power and any minister who contended that he did have this power should not, I think, be in a democracy but should be somewhere else.
We are ready to protect the farmers and give them the advantages that they have; either to keep them under the present formula or under any other formula to which everybody, or the majority, would agree. I really do not
mind,	and I am sure the farmers don't mind; only those who are ready to exploit politically the symbol of Crowsnest pass rates discuss this question.

Yesterday in the House, Madam Chairman, as reported at page 5676 of Hansard, in response to a question by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, the Minister of Justice in charge of the Wheat Board said:
I indicated that in my view the test whether such a change could be made was really dependent upon the will of the farmers themselves.
I would like to ask the Minister of Transport what mechanism will be established to determine the will of the farmers. Will it be the minister in charge of the Wheat Board who makes that decision? It really worries me, if that is the case. I would like to remind the Minister of Transport that it was not our party or any other opposition party in the House which first started the question about what the government was doing about the Crowsnest pass agreement. It was the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, in his speech in Edmonton, who first said there might be some changes made to it. Now he says that any changes would depend upon the will of the farmers. How do we interpret that will? Is the minister thinking of a plebiscite? Is the minister in charge of the Wheat Board going to interpret their will? I ask this question because his interpretation of their will is often different from
mine,	or different from that of the farm organizations. After all, you are the Minister of Transport, not him.
I am very tired of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board meddling with the Minister of Agriculture, meddling with the Minister of Transport, meddling with several other ministers. Is he a czar? Is he the king of the
29561-20'/i

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
government? What does he mean? I want to know from you what he means when he says he will interpret the will of the farmers.

Madam Chairman, I think that on the principle involved here nobody can contest that it is very important to know the will of the farmers. I do not think you oppose the will of the farmers, as I am sure the hon. member will agree. What the hon. member is asking is, how you would define, or how you would get to know the will of the farmers. I suggest he asks the Minister of Justice exactly what he means and what method he proposes to use.

Is not the minister we are questioning today the Minister of Transport? Surely to goodness this falls under your purview as it is a freight rate question. If he is going to decide to meddle with your department, why in the devil don't you slap his hand? You should be making that decision, not the Minister of Justice; right?
Such a decision, a very important one, will be made by the cabinet after a recommendation of one minister whose name, now, is the Minister of Transport; and nobody else.

I have it very clearly, then, that it is the Minister of Transport who will make the recommendations regarding the Crowsnest rate, regarding transportation matters, not the Minister of Justice. It will be you.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I should like to remind the hon. gentleman that he is supposed to address the Chair.

I should like to go back to the subject of dredging and ask the minister a question or two. I was amazed when the alleged bid-rigging-I say "alleged" because nothing has been proven-came to light and charges were laid as to how it could have happened, how the government could find itself in a position where something was alleged to have been going on for such a long time and on such a scale. I think the answer came when the Minister of Public Works disclosed the guidelines which have intended to protect the public in the future.
Apparently there are dredging contracts let by the Department of Public Works, by the Department of Transport, by the National Harbours Board and by the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. As a result of this, as the government now recognizes by having set up the safeguarding committee, there is not sufficient expertise, apparatus or machinery available in Public Works, Transport or anywhere else to protect the public. As a result of the lack of adequate machinery in the Department of Transport, for example, there was no way in which the public could be protected. The people in the department had no suspicion that in fact the bids were so far above what they should be that bid-rigging was quite possible.
I would like to know how the Minister of Transport can attempt to justify this fragmentation of authority in the field of dredging. Some of it is done in Transport, some in Public Works, some here and some there. How can the minister justify this situation having continued, I do not know for how long? When he became minister in 1973, for

example, he had reason to be suspicious about some things in Hamilton. Shortly thereafter he had reason to become suspicious about the St. Lawrence River dredging. Yet the system continued. Nobody in the government, nobody in his department, seemed to make any move in order to improve the administrative machinery or to create some unit in the government which would know enough about dredging to ensure that the bids were appropriate, and thus protect the public.
Despite the belated move the government has made to set up an improvised cabinet committee, I charge that the public of Canada has paid very dearly for the fragmentation of authority in the area of dredging. The lack of expertise in the Department of Transport meant that apparently no accurate judgment could be made as to whether bids in connection with dredging were appropriate or not, or whether contracts for the salvage of a ship were in line or not. The government apparently had no idea that there was something seriously wrong with regard to the bidding or with regard to dredging generally.
I suggest this could not have happened at all if the departments concerned had been able to assess properly, or even estimate properly, what the appropriate bids should have been in connection with these contracts. Yet the system went on year after year despite warnings by the Auditor General that contracts were running over. I make the charge that the government did not take the trouble to protect the public by setting up the necessary machinery, and as far as I can understand it failed to provide adequate measures to protect the public after contracts had been let.

Madam Chairman, perhaps I can be as blunt as the Leader of the Opposition. Not only this government, but all governments prior to this one have been following exactly the same regulations and laws. We ask for bids and we choose the lowest, unless the lowest bidder is not in a position to do the work. If he does not have the machinery required or the ability to do the work, then I think any government would tell him that he is not going to get the job. That has been the practice.
The hon. member for Annapolis Valley referred a few minutes ago to some contracts that were given in 1963. That is when Hon. Leon Balcer was minister of transport, so he should check into that. I do not know why he did not verify that beforehand.
I would be as prudent as the Leader of the Opposition. If the charges are founded, then it means there has been collusion to cheat the government. That is not the first time it has happened; it happens everywhere in the world. There is no way you can protect yourself against four, five or six firms who agree to get together and establish a floor. This was revealed in Hamilton by a commission over which I have no jurisdiction at all. The contract there was awarded by the harbour commission of Hamilton, not by the Department of Transport, and I think the hon. gentleman should ask why this commission did not make a better check than it did. As far as the other cases are concerned, hon. members will have to wait until the trial is over to see whether there has been any collusion. That is all I can say.
May 13, 1975

The other day I received quite a high bid for a project in a city in the west, and there was only the one bid. I spent at least 15 days consulting all kinds of people in Justice, and so forth, and I asked them what I should do. They told me that in that particular city there was nobody else who could do the job. We assess what the job is worth, and they told me that the job was worth it and that that is what we should do; otherwise we would have to go to Vancouver, Montreal or Toronto.
I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that this means there are some weaknesses and holes in the system. However, we now have some new rules under which all bids are submitted to Justice to see whether they can see something we have not seen. We are trying to be more strict. If there is a big difference between what we assess and the bid of the lowest bidder, then in such case perhaps we should scrap the whole thing and start all over again or tell the firm in question that we suspect there is something wrong.
Perhaps this sort of rigging has happened in the past; I do not know. The inquiry may reveal that the same situation has existed in many other cases. Perhaps it took place under the right hon. member for Prince Albert. I have no way of knowing; but he was applying exactly the same regulations.

Madam Chairman, I do not know whether it happened under Sir Robert Borden or under Sir John A. Macdonald, but we are talking about the present administration. I cannot make a charge that there was collusion, but I am assuming that charges have been laid by the government. I make the assertion that if there was collusion in bid-rigging in connection with dredging contracts with the Department of Transport, then it was because the Department of Transport was a sitting duck for such bid-rigging and collusion: it did not have the expertise and apparatus to know whether or not it was being taken to the cleaners.
I ask the minister, through you, Madam Chairman, why this was allowed to continue for a year or so after the minister became suspicious. It was not until the whole thing was out in the open that the Minister of Public Works announced in this House the appointment of a committee, which itself is probably quite inadequate.
The minister says that something happened in Hamilton. I am not blaming him for that. The whole organization behind dredging operations for harbour commissions and so on may very well need looking into. But I am asking him this. Apart from talking about what may have happened 20 or 40 years ago, is there any way he can explain to this committee and to the people of Canada why he, as minister, and why his predecessor and the government as a whole, allowed to continue an obviously inadequate system of administering dredging contracts, one which apparently permitted the Government of Canada and the people of Canada to be taken to the cleaners for years?

Madam Chairman, I must correct something which has been said by the Leader of the Opposition. I do not know whether he was including me when he said we knew something was wrong in the awarding of dredging contracts a year ago. If so, I tell him
Business of Supply
that that is not true. The first time I heard about that was at the beginning of March. Immediately I took action, as I did in the case of Air Canada. But one year ago I was not aware of anything of this kind. If he contends that the Minister of Public Works knew, I would be happy to be here when he puts the question to the minister, because I do not think he is the type of man to let that kind of thing go on.
Madam Chairman, I am not going to get sidetracked by charges of who did what, or who did not know what.
You are the one who brought that up.

I am saying that the system in the Department of Transport-and I dare say the same applies to the system in Public Works-was very inadequate to protect the public, and that there was no justification for allowing it to continue through the years, particularly in view of the reports of the Auditor General. As I say, I do not intend to be sidetracked by statements about who did what, or about what the minister found out subsequently.

Madam Chairman, the system which existed in Transport is the same system that existed everywhere in the government and in all governments I know of in Canada. It is the system of asking for tenders and bids. I do not know what the future has in store for those who might be involved, but up until now no civil servant has been involved, accused, charged or even suspected of wrongdoing. When four or five firms control a whole industry, they do not need any civil servants; they just decide themselves what they are going to do.
That damns you all the more for not keeping abreast of it.

Then in one case it became apparent, the police found out and we acted as quickly as we could. There may be other situations and perhaps hon. members opposite will be able to give us some help. There are certain industries where it is almost impossible to find a second bidder. For example, if you want some transistors, outside of IBM of Canada where would you go? Where would the competition come from? Even if you went to the United States, perhaps you would have to go to IBM even there. Certain industries are monopolized, so we have to be very careful. As I say, we have followed the rules. No civil servants have been charged or suspected of wrongdoing.
I do not see why the Leader of the Opposition would make that kind of attack. Perhaps he is suggesting that the prevailing system in Canada is not foolproof and we should see how we can improve it. That is right, and that is what we are trying to do.

I have just one more sentence, Madam Chairman. The system is inadequate and the government has finally recognized this in setting up a makeshift kind of citizens' protective committee. The system is inadequate to anyone who has made an examination, if only

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
because of the fact the Department of Public Works was responsible for part of it, the Minister of Transport for another part of it, and somebody else for another part of it. We were just taken to the cleaners.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. The time allotted to the hon. Leader of the Opposition has now expired.

Before recognizing the hon. member for Davenport, I should like to point out that the time of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville was cut short by one minute, so perhaps I might recognize that hon. member for one question.

If I have one minute, I will take 20 seconds and the minister can take 40 seconds. If there are any changes whatsoever which will limit the benefits of the Crowsnest pass rates, will those changes take place before Mr. Justice Hall has had time to report on western transportation problems, with recommendations to the government; or will they, if there are any, come after Mr. Justice Hall's report?
If you want my opinion, and you will understand that is all I can give, it is no.

Madam Chairman, there are three brief questions I should like to direct to the minister. The first relates to whether the Minister of Transport is playing an active role in relation to urban growth by providing Canadians who are prepared to live in smaller centres in the neighbourhood of metropolitan regions with adequate commuter services that would permit them to work in large metropolises.
It is quite clear that we have now reached the stage where certain cities are becoming very large, and there are certain towns and small cities in Canada where Canadians might buy homes and settle at a lower cost while still working at their jobs in the large industrial centres. There is a growing body of Canadians who feel that the urban growth of our metropolitan areas can be slowed down if we adopt a transportation policy which will encourage the growth of smaller centres. Is the minister actively involved with the Minister of State for Urban Affairs in developing a policy of that kind?
My second question stems from an observation I have made over the years of bus terminals, railway stations and airports. On the face of it, one wonders whether the allocation of taxpayers' money for travelling Canadians is proportionately divided between those travelling by ground transportation as opposed to those travelling by air. In other words, putting it in reverse, one gets the impression that we are investing a substantial amount of taxpayers' funds for that portion of the public travelling by air which is much smaller than that provided for those who travel by train or bus.
One gets the impression that we pay much greater attention to and place more emphasis and financial support on air travel for those who use that service than we do in respect of bus or train transportation. I would be very grateful if the minister could indicate whether this is a

superficial appearance, or whether in fact there is something in what I have suggested.
My final question relates to a local matter. In Toronto we have a large project called the Metro Centre which has been in the hands of a corporation called Metro Centre Development. This involves large tracts of lands which are publicly owned, including land owned by Canadian National and Canadian Pacific. I understand that the current agreement on Metro Centre expires in November of this year. If a new contract is to be arrived at following the expiration of the existing one, it would be helpful to know whether the Ministry of Transport and Canadian National will insist that the publicly-owned land remain under public control and managed, in terms of planning and utilization, by the local municipality rather than by the private developer who is developing the specific tracts of land. Those are my questions.

Madam Chairman, I was not involved in this discussion until January 20, if my memory serves me well, when Premier Davis invited me to Toronto to discuss this matter with him, his officials and some of the senior officers of the Ministry of Transport. Since then we have been looking into this matter and a report will probably be produced within a few weeks, at which time we will know exactly what is to happen concerning the ownership of this land. I have my own opinion on this, and when I get that report I will see how my opinion compares with the opinion expressed in it. That is the situation at the present time. We are awaiting the report of this study, and it is only when we receive it that we will indicate exactly what we are going to do.

Madam Chairman, I will be very brief and I will stay with one aspect of transportation, that is, the proposed Pickering airport in the Toronto area. I only have two or three brief questions, but before I ask them I should like to summarize the background of several contradictions I believe exist in statements by the Minister of Transport and the Prime Minister regarding this proposed airport.
It is a publicly known fact that several surveys have been conducted in the metropolitan area. The Elliott Research Corporation carried out one survey, the Toronto Star carried out another, and a poll survey was conducted by the Canadian Facts Company Limited. Within the metropolitan area, 61.4 per cent of those who had an opinion were opposed to the airport decision. Even in the Malton impact area, which the government argues will benefit from reduced noise as a result of the second airport, the majority of those who had an opinion were against the airport.
The Ministry of Transport's traffic forecasts do not reflect the current economic and fuel picture and the recent decline in international air travel. Furthermore, the government has made absolutely no effort to spread peak hour load which is the real measure of airport capacity at the Malton airport today. The Gibson commission, for example, concluded that provision of terminal capacity at Malton would not be a problem until 1985, even assuming the inflated Ministry of Transport's passenger forecasts which will not be realized for many years after 1985. So that is an inflated figure.
May 13, 1975

Further terminal needs, should they become evident over the next decade, could be met either by more efficient use of lands within the present airport boundary, such as by achieving the same ratio of passenger handling capacity to required land area as the present Terminal 1, or by annexing a moderate amount of vacant industrial land. There is definitely no spreading of noise involved in the placing of extra terminals at the present Malton airport.
Runway capacity at Malton is no problem except during the peak hour when strong north-south winds limit use to one runway, 14-32. Opening one runway at Pickering in the east-west direction does not solve the runway capacity problem. When additional runway capacity is required at Malton, a fourth independent runway in the north-south direction within Malton's existing boundaries could be added. The minister's department admits that at a separation of 4,400 feet, no more people will be affected than with the three-runway situation. The airport inquiry commission agrees that with the addition of such a runway, Malton can handle Ministry of Transport forecasts to beyond 1990.
It can be assumed, also, that due to technological advances noise will continue to decrease as long as realistic assumptions are made about the phasing out of DC-8 type aircraft and some control over night flights, particularly of noisy aircraft, is exerted even if no new noise technology is introduced. This has far more effect on noise than the government's plan in respect of Pickering. In addition, if the government pursues its own proposal to have aircraft meet standards similar to FAR 36 at Malton by 1980, the noise reduction will be even more dramatic. Once all aircraft meet FAR 36 standards, the additional beneficial effect of opening a second airport is very small.
The minister gave the following answer to a question I asked in the House on February 21 regarding the airport. He stated, as reported at 3436 of Hansard:
If the hon. gentleman can bring some kind of evidence to show that the majority of the population is against the airport, I am ready to revise the whole thing.
This evidence has been presented very emphatically through the media and through different polls. I expect my first question is obvious. Why is the minister not sticking to the statement he made in this House, along with the statement of the Prime Minister, to the effect that if there were even 51 per cent of the people around the Pickering area against the airport, the government would reconsider the matter and look into the different options? Surely an airport as expensive as this-it is expensive and I will be asking a couple of questions about the expense-is not needed at this time; the money could be handed over for the purpose of helping the housing situation which is drastic in the Toronto area. I believe the number of housing starts in that area has been reduced in the past year by 60 per cent.
The first question I would ask is whether the minister is taking a different position now from the one he took in the statement he made in the House, and outside the House, and one the Prime Minister took in his statements.

Mr. Chairman, the answer is very simple. I have no idea how the inquiry was con-
Business of Supply
ducted, who was consulted or what was the form of the inquiry. One thing we did in respect of Pickering which we did not do in respect of any other airport, and certainly not in respect of Mirabel, was that before we chose the site of Pickering we had many consultations, including consultations with the government of Ontario, and everybody thought it was the best place. When I say "everybody," I do not refer to the people around Pickering but I refer to the government of Ontario and those who are involved in the building of the airport.
So it is one thing if the population of Ontario or of greater Toronto does not want this airport, but no Gallup poll or anything of that kind was conducted which would suggest this. I did not need to conduct an inquiry: our information was very instructive. The results the hon. member produces in the House may have some bearing, but we had the Gibson inquiry and its report. In that report, the arguments were made by a person who was in no way tied to the government and who, with two colleagues, gave an opinion and answers to questions which to my mind are much better than the opinions cited by the hon. gentleman.

Mr. Chairman, of course, much of the opinion stated in the Gibson inquiry report has changed since the inquiry took place. So far as the polls are concerned, surely the Toronto Star poll conducted by the Canadian Facts Company Limited would not be considered a one-sided opinion. This is a very important matter and a costly affair which I am sure will not help the majority of the people of Toronto, because they are still looking for better housing rather than a second airport. In view of this, would the minister be willing to have the government conduct its own poll concerning the situation in the Toronto area, to determine whether the people there are for, or against, that airport? I know the minister wishes to abide by the wishes of the people of that city and of Canada, so perhaps he will take it upon himself to conduct a poll of his own.

Mr. Chairman, I think we have done all that can normally be done in the circumstances. We even had a special inquiry. Witnesses have been heard, briefs have been presented and there has even been cross-examination of witnesses. The same conclusion was reached as that of the ministry. So far as I am concerned, the decision has been made. If another government, another minister, or someone else should change his mind, that is all right; but so far as I am concerned, this is a closed case and I will not go back on it.

So it can be taken that the minister either unintentionally misled the House when he made the statement or has changed his mind. The possibility exists, if sufficient pressure is put on him by the majority of the people, that he might change his mind again so far as the airport is concerned.
I should like to ask a question about the cost of the airport. Early in the year 1974, the minister stated that the Pickering airport, including construction and land, would cost $204 million. In an answer to a written question I placed on the order paper, which I received on April 7, the department stated that the authorized cost for the construction of the international airport and related facilities

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
in land approved by the government on February 20, 1975, is slightly in excess of $200 million. This relates to the figure of $204 million; but there is an addendum which says that no airport construction is included in this figure. The figure previous to this, of $204 million, included the construction.
As well, on February 20 the minister said that a runway and appropriate passenger terminal and related facilities would be built. Given the existing examples of passenger terminals at Malton and Edmonton international airports, where passengers are forced to trek considerable distances, would the minister offer his definition of an appropriate passenger terminal and the separate cost involved for the construction of the terminal facilities to begin this year, or whenever that may be? What will be the additional cost?

Unfortunately, I am not an architect. I cannot say exactly what kind of terminal will be built there. I presume that we will receive some designs and suggestions from technicians of all kinds, including engineers, and so forth. Then we will make up our minds. But if I am asked exactly what I mean by an appropriate terminal, I presume it would be a terminal which would receive passengers who land in Pickering. We would try to avoid what happened in Terminal 2 and have something which is convenient for the people who are going to use it. When we have the design, if the hon. member wishes I will be happy to receive him in my office. My office is not far away, and I will show the design to him.

Mr. Chairman, that is very kind of the minister. It is assumed that the proposed airport will be an international airport. The question, of course, is whether the nednister or the government have received any assurances that international airlines will operate out of Pickering airport, seeing that the airport as it now stands in the plans will only have one runway. Several air carriers use international airports. These air carriers would be in the air at all times, and having one runway is like being half pregnant without wanting to be pregnant in the first place.

Mr. Chairman, we in Canada tell foreign airlines where they can land, and in turn we negotiate with France, for example, or Great Britain, as to which airport we are supposed to use. They told us where we could land; we did not tell them where we would land. We are not free to land just anywhere in Berlin or elsewhere. This is in the agreement, and I think this is what we will do with the airlines.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I have to interrupt the hon. member because the time allotted to him has expired.
I have just a short, final question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That can be done if the committee accepts it, and if it can be done in a few seconds I am ready to accept the question.
Agreed.

It will just take a few seconds. I know that the minister has a great deal of interest in the development of STOL aircraft and STOL routes such as the route existing between Ottawa and Montreal. At least he had interest in this. Does this mean that with the additional airport at Pickering, the interest toward the development of STOL aircraft in Toronto-I am speaking specifically of the possibility of Toronto island as an airport for STOL aircraft-will be laid aside? Will this become secondary to Pickering?

This is an experiment we are doing with Twin-Otters between Ottawa and Montreal. To this date we are very satisfied with the success of this experiment. We do not have all the elements. Some airlines have already asked for permission to operate STOL systems between certain Canadian cities. We are not ready to allow that because our experiment is not completed. Nothing has been excluded. We have not excluded the island in Toronto, nor the island in Montreal; and if ever we decide to have a STOL program for those two cities, those might be the proper places to have them.

Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the previous speaker because his last question ties in exactly with what I want to discuss with the minister this afternoon. I would like to state that as far as I and, I think, many members of this House are concerned, the topic of transport is probably one of the most all-encompassing topics up for discussion at any time, because through the transport policies of governments of Canada this nation was brought together in the first place. It is through transport policy that it has kept together, and through transport policy in the future it will be determined how well this nation remains together as a corporate entity.
I want to direct my remarks to the minister, not on the primary level of air traffic-Air Canada or CP Air-but to take a look at the over-all scheme for regional air carriers and the use, as the previous member was discussing, of the hub and spoke concept of STOL air service. In my opinion the success or failure of transport in the future will depend on the proper integration of all types of transport, whether it be by land, sea, air, rail or bus, and in particular the phasing in of a comprehensive and well run hub and spoke STOL air service; because I think the success of our national railways in years past has been primarily through use of feeder lines, the small lines which were brought in to bring people from outlying areas into the centres of communication which joined up with the transcontinental systems which ran from coast to coast. I believe the hub and spoke air concept will become the feeder lines of transportation in years to come.
As the minister knows, Canada, and in particular the De Havilland Aircraft Corporation, have been world leaders in the development of the STOL concept, first with the De Havilland DHC 6 Twin Otter and now with the recent unveiling of the DHC 7 and 7-R, the second generation of STOL aircraft. It is here in Canada that the augmenter-wing concept was designed, and while we are world leaders in the design and development of these aircraft and of the hub and spoke concept of transportation, our failure to use this concept of proper advantage where it would fit is something I find rather deplorable.
May 13, 1975

For the betterment of our own population I do not feel the very concept we have developed to such a high degree has been used as it should be. I would ask the minister to give this House, at some time, an indication of the progress made by his department in adopting this important concept of communications into a national transport picture and in putting it into implementation on a nationwide and regional scale.
I would like also to point out my concern, and the concern of the people I represent, about the continuing policy of our national railways of branch line abandonment both in the passenger field and the freight field. I would ask the minister to make every effort to encourage both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific to stop completely the withdrawal of what I consider to be an essential element of cohesion across this country. I speak with the knowledge which comes from representing an area where the withdrawal of rail service, particularly in the passenger field, has taken place and where the effects of that withdrawal are still suffered.
I would point out that had it not been for the work of at least one private company-I refer to Bruce Coach Lines of Kincardine, Ontario-in picking up the slack which developed in the transportation system which was available to the people of western Ontario and to my particular section of the country, we would indeed be in a very difficult position at this time. Since that time the bus service facilities have been upgraded and increased. As a result, the people have started to use it. The travelling time between Kincardine and Toronto is now 3 Vi hours by bus, but it still takes 5 Vi hours by rail.
I hope the minister will give us his views on this serious situation and indicate whether this practice by the railways can be reversed, if not stopped. As a private enterprise, Canadian Pacific Railway has to be concerned with the return on investment, but Canadian National Railways is a little different in that for the most part it is financed by public money. It therefore has a duty and responsibility to provide the transportation that the people so desperately need.
I should like to return to the question of STOL. It is interesting to note that transporting people and commodities economically and efficiently is one of the things that this country does best. One reason for this is that our geographical footprint dictates it. We have 3,852,000 square miles of land mass to cover; and for those of our friends who are interested in metric measurement, that is 10,015,000 square kilometres. This includes large metropolitan areas, mountain ranges, plains and inland waters, so it has been an absolute necessity that we develop this expertise. The fact is, however, that the expertise is more essential now than at any other time in our country's history.
I should like to turn, now, to the regional development of the STOL concept. If STOL is to work, I believe it will work best in a number of networks of well planned, regional services interconnecting through the national air carriers which will provide the type of service this nation requires. The type of system operating up and down the Norwegian coast to provide isolated hamlets with air service to the larger centres, and thence to Oslo, the capital,
Business of Supply
and other centres of population and industry is an example of what can be done. The effect has been to decentralize some of the large cities. This might be useful to us, with such large centres as Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver growing the way they are. We must get the people out of these centralized communities into places which need to build up their industry and population.
I should like to ask the minister what his department thinks can be done about the Toronto island airport. To my way of thinking, this airport is absolutely essential to provide the hub and spoke concept for southwestern and central Ontario. It is ideally situated and is currently licensed for STOL use on a VFR basis, but must be upgraded to a STOL IFR standard.
Not with that big needle sticking up in the middle of the city.

That is outside the approach patterns that would be used for STOL aircraft. In closing, Mr. Chairman, I would like to put forward some statistics about STOL. First of all, it saves fuel. The DASH 7 will save up to $100,000 a year on 200-mile routes over the operation of the DC-9-about a 64 per cent saving in fuel.
We are all worried about the ecology and the emission of pollutants. The average car, on a 200-mile trip carrying 1.25 passengers-I will never figure out why they use 1.25 passengers; I can see one passenger, but not IV* passengers-would produce about 27 pounds of pollutant per passenger. The DC-9, on a 200-mile trip, would produce about 1.14 pounds; the bus, one pound per passenger and the train about nine-tenths of a pound. The DASH 7 would produce only six-tenths of a pound per passenger, on a 200-mile trip. That is something to think about, Mr. Chairman.
The DASH 7 also saves time, and today time is money. Let us take, as an example, a trip from the Parliament Buildings here to downtown Montreal, the Bonaventure Hotel. The total time for the trip by conventional air traffic, using a taxi from here to the airport and from the airport in Montreal, is two hours and three minutes. That is taxi time, terminal time and flying time. By STOL, using the Twin Otter plane, the total time is one hour and 22 minutes. I believe it is the answer to many of the transportation problems not only in Ontario but throughout the country. It could be used in other provinces, and to put it into operation would only cost about the same as it would to build two miles of four-lane highway in southwestern and central Ontario. Tied in with the proper rail and bus service, it would provide the people with a transportation system second to none.
If the minister has time, I would appreciate some answers to my questions, and if he has not I should like to hear from him by letter.

Mr. Chairman, I only have three minutes so I am going to answer rapidly. We are co-operating with the province of Ontario on the hub and spoke concept. As far as STOL is concerned, we have to complete our experiments. At the moment, we cannot use the DASH 7 because it is being tested and will not be ready for a few months or a year. The concept is of

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
interest, and that is why we have invested so much money in it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a few questions to the minister concerning the dredging contract at Ile-d'Orleans. Initially, this contract was for dredging in the main ship channel of the St. Lawrence River below Quebec in the reach commonly known as the North Traverse, extending from St. Jean, Ile-d'Orleans to Sault au Cochon, consisting of a quantity of approximately 14 million cubic yards. The contract was to be for a period of three years commencing the summer of 1971. The estimated cost of the contract was $20,860,000, with the basis of payment being $1.49 per cubic yard.
In response to public advertisements, three bids were received. One was from J. P. Porter Ltd., McNamara Co. Ltd. and Marine Industries Ltd., a joint venture, for $20,860,000. One was from Canadian Dredge and Dock Ltd. and T. C. Gorman Ltd., a combine of two, for $28,140,000. The third was from C. A. Pitts Engineering Construction Ltd., for $30,100,000. Authority for the Department of Transport to enter into a contract with the lowest bidder was given by Treasury Board minute 706359 dated August 30, 1971, and subsequently a formal contract was entered into with the successful bidder. Since the department's estimate is identical to the price quoted by the lowest bidder, would the minister confirm my research of this item and explain this coincidence to the committee? That is my first question.
My second question relates to the minister's comments concerning the Hamilton Harbour Commission, made just a few moments ago in response to questions raised by my leader. The Hamilton Harbour Commission and the Toronto Harbour Commission are corporate bodies which are audited by the municipal auditor of the municipality which has a major interest in the commission. The minister, under the Harbour Commissions Act, may authorize an inspection of the books and records of the harbour commissions, but the Department of Transport financial audit and review branch has never made any audits or reviews of these commissions. To the best of my knowledge, the government has never asked the Auditor General or any of his staff to examine the records of the harbour commissions.
Since the present audit system of the Auditor General is not designed to detect fraud and deliberate collusion, the onus in my view is on the minister and on the government to take the necessary action. Will the minister inform this committee why he never authorized an inspection of the books and records of the harbour commissions I have mentioned?

Mr. Chairman, I will need to verify the hon. member's assertion that we must verify the books of the harbour commissions. I always thought that the cities were supposed not only to supervise but to award contracts. I may be mistaken. I want to check. I should like the hon. gentleman to tell me what part of the act authorizes us to inspect those books in the city in which the commission is located. I think the city of Hamil-

ton, which awarded this contract, is also supposed to supervise.

Mr. Chairman, it is my understanding that the minister, under the Harbour Commissions Act, RSC, chapter H-l, may authorize an inspection of the books and records of harbour commissions. He has that authority but has never exercised the authority which is in RSC, chapter H-l. Surely his departmental officials can verify that statement right now.
Secondly, I should like him to answer my first question concerning the coincidence whereby the consortium composed of J. P. Porter Ltd., McNamara Company Ltd. and Marine Industries Ltd. could come up with a figure of $20,860,000 for the dredging to which I referred, exactly the same figure as estimated by the department. I think the committee deserves some explanation of that.

Mr. Chairman, I think you must consider that this is part of the trial or the case which is before the courts now, and I think the committee will surely have an opportunity to learn when the judgment comes down.
The judgment?

Oh, yes; a judgment will be handed down. Surely the hon. member is not asking me to give him an opinion when the matter is before the judge. The judge can hear witnesses, and he has not yet made up his mind.
Come, now! This is public information.

Mr. Chairman, by leaning on the fact that this case is presently before the courts, the minister is not playing fair with the committee. It is true that the vouchers and departmental files have been seized by the RCMP and that a writ has been issued; it is true that these documents are presently being held and are under investigation by the RCMP. But the questions I raised surely come within the authority of the minister and the department. After all, the bids to which I referred, the public tenders which I mentioned, are public knowledge. Public tenders were called. The three companies, making up a consortium, bid $20,860,000 for this project, exactly, the amount estimated by the department. There must have been a coincidence as between the department's estimate and the figure bid by the lowest bidder, namely, the consortium made up of the Porter Company, the McNamara Company and Marine Industries.
I do not see how the minister can refuse to answer by suggesting the matter is before the courts. I am asking him to explain how this coincidence concerning the bids occurred. For example, did someone in the department tell Porter, McNamara and Marine Industries, "Our estimate is $20,860,000"? Did someone in the minister's department volunteer this information? Did these companies ask some official how low an estimate the department itself had made for this work? Because the next highest bid was $28,140,000 the third bid was $30,100,000. There may have been collusion; I do not say there was but there may have been. Certainly, someone was in the confidence of the minister's staff if there was a tender for this contract
May 13, 1975

which was identical to the figure estimated by the minister's officials. I suggest that such a coincidence is unique and can be explained without infringing on the matter now before the courts.

Mr. Chairman, I am in a difficult position. I am sure the hon. member was honest in his research. But how can I explain it if the RCMP and the courts cannot explain it? I do not know how I can explain it. The RCMP have investigated this case and looked into the books of these companies and of other companies-even in my riding if you want to know. They searched everywhere. At no time did they charge or indicate that a civil servant was involved. The whole thing is now before the courts. It may be pure coincidence. If so, we will say it is a coincidence and that is all. If fraud is involved, I say to the hon. member that the police have investigated and that the courts are acting. So do not ask me why there is a coincidence unless you assume that the whole thing happened in my office. I am sure that is not what the hon. member assumes.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask one short question? Does the minister concede that the estimate by his officials of $20,860,000 is exactly the same figure that was paid to the consortium when they signed the contract?
Mr. Chairman, we will have to check.
After he has checked, will the minister make that information available to the committee?
Yes, certainly.

Mr. Chairman, I believe most members will agree that the Minister of Transport heads one of the most important ministries of government and has one of the most important portfolios in this House. Transportation affects all Canadians. The ministry is a grass roots ministry, a department which provides service to more Canadians than any other of which I am aware.
I am a new member, as you know, Mr. Chairman; an independent without party affiliation. Nevertheless, the minister has generally co-operated with me; other ministers have, too. Actually, I have already invited the minister down to the Atlantic provinces, and particularly to the city of Moncton, so that he can see first-hand our transportation problems in the area instead of leaving it to bureaucrats. I might say that this invitation is extended to the minister's confreres. We hope they will hold a cabinet meeting in Moncton this year as this is an anniversary year for the city.
I marvel at the huge staff of the Ministry of Transport and at the huge staffs of Crown agencies and corporations which come under its authority. How many persons hold executive positions in the ministry, its agencies and Crown corporations? What is the total amount paid in salaries to them and their support staff, and overburden expenses? I imagine many members of this House ask themselves what do these people do. What is the evidence of what they do? Possibly bureaucrats have too much to say, not enough to do and assume little or no responsibility for the high wages they receive.
Business of Supply
We hear of studies for this, and studies for that, and a study of this study and another study of that study-all at substantial cost to the taxpayer; all in addition to the cost of salaries of overburdens. We need action, and we need it soon.
Maritimers are still concerned about their freight rates. The consumer is paying the shot. When will the Ministry of Transport unveil a national transportation policy and a regional transportation policy? Will the minister advise what amounts have been provided for rail line relocation, in particular for the proposed rail line relocation in the Moncton area?
I wish to ask some questions with regard to transportation problems in my constituency. I know some of the national problems; however, Moncton is the transportation centre of the maritimes. First, there is the problem of CNR pensioners and widows. I suggest to the minister that this is a problem of government because in the Atlantic provinces the railways were formerly operated by the Canadian government. I suggest the government has a responsibility to these people. Second, there is need for an improved and enlarged CNR station in Moncton. Colloquially, in Moncton, that station is called the musical shoebox. It certainly fits the description. I am told that regularly tracks are out of commission in the Atlantic region. The rolling-stock is not kept up to date. There are very serious matters concerning the safety of passengers, cargo and materials.
We also hear of lay-offs. The condition of the equipment, the rolling-stock, the trackage and the lay-offs are not consistent. I suggest if there are no lay-offs, the railway gives the excuse that they do not have the men to do the job. With the lay-offs, I suggest this is an excellent time for the railways to bring their equipment, goods and trackage up to standard. I suggest the minister has a responsibility to the public on these matters of safety.
There are other matters in so far as the budget of the Department of Transport is concerned. Recently on the order paper there were items with reference to the cost of bilingualism in the CNR and Air Canada. I would like to know the cost of implementing bilingualism and any training in the Department of Transport and the Crown corporations and agencies under that department. This matter of the cost of bilingualism is completely out of hand. It has recently been revealed that upward of $3 million was spent on this by CNR. In Air Canada, therefore, we can assume it was $4 million.
Recently, Mr. Keith Spicer, the Commissioner of Official Languages, reported that languages should be taught in school. It has occurred to me that finally this gentleman, like many members of this House, is now beginning to see the light. Linguistic problems are educational problems and should be solved within the school system of this country and not within the government. It should be done in an integrated, non-separate, uniform school system with both English and French languages being taught to all our children together. You cannot do it by teaching people at age 30 to 50 or 60.
I raise this matter here because employees of CNR, Air Canada, other Crown agencies and the Department of

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
Transport-and, for that matter, other departments of government-are in a state of fear as a result of the policy and method adopted for the implementation of bilingualism. It is unfair, unreasonable and results in poor labour relations and costs that are a burden. It is creating disunity and is separating our country. It is destroying it. These funds could, and should be used to create productive employment. The present policy detracts substantially from the service now provided by Air Canada and CNR employees. It is reducing the morale of the employees and this results in lack of initiative and fear in jobs. Bilingualism in air traffic control is creating a real problem. I suggest that this is an international, English fact and we should leave it alone.
Another matter which concerns my constituents is the reduced air service provided to the city of Moncton and, in fact, the whole province of New Brunswick. There is no direct air service between the nation's capital and the province of New Brunswick. In conjunction with the Greater Moncton Chamber of Commerce and the Moncton city council, I met with Air Canada officials. A suggestion has been made to Air Canada in order to rectify the problem. I ask the minister to use his good offices to have this matter rectified. This is one case where Air Canada can do something to produce revenue. That is something Air Canada, CNR and some other agencies and corporations of government are reluctant to do. It might mean a little diplomacy, but it can be done.
Further, for years in southeastern New Brunswick we have been without adequate passenger facilities and baggage facilities. The runways should be repaired, improved and extended. In some cases, aircraft have to come in on the wrong runway. That should not happen in this day and age. The passenger terminal is packed. Customs facilities are inadequate and should be improved. The services and facilities of that airport are taxed to capacity. I want to know from the minister if provision has been made for these additional facilities. They are needed now. Incidentally, if there are any more problems in the controversy with regard to the Pickering airport, I suggest that the minister divert the funds allocated for the Pickering airport to the needed improvements and extension of services and facilities of the Moncton airport and other needs in the Moncton and Atlantic region.
In addition, the matter of a national transportation policy and a regional transportation policy, whether the minister agrees or not, and the problem of urban transportation in its fullest and most complete definition and interpretation cannot be forgotten. These matters are most essential: they deserve the attention of the minister and his department.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member will understand that I cannot answer all the questions or deal with all the subjects he has raised, particularly with regard to bilingualism. It would take much more time that we have at the moment. There will be another opportunity. I think the hon. member is interested in knowing whether the facilities at the Moncton airport will be improved. I can say there is something in the estimates and we hope to make these improvements this year. I think the amount for this year is just over $2.5 million. With regard to how that amount will be spent, I

will have to check with the department to see exactly what they have in mind. I know there is another amount provided for in the next fiscal year. I promise the hon. member that some day I will visit Moncton so that I can see for myself what is going on. Does the hon. member want to ask a question?

Regarding what the minister has just said with respect to the $2.5 million, is that for the aircraft control relocation or does it include extention of the terminal facilities, including passenger and baggage facilities?

Mr. Chairman, that is what I want to verify. If the hon. member has no objection, and if I cannot give him the information before the end of the day, I will write to him tomorrow telling him exactly what we intend to do with that amount of money.
