speechtext: At this point I should inform the committee of the questions to be raised at the time of the adjournment. They are as follows: the hon. member for Parkdale-Immigration; the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants-Public Service; the hon. member for Simcoe North-National Parks.

Mr. Chairman, as a preamble I should like to thank the Minister of Transport and his staff for their co-operation in the past. In particular, I wish to express my thanks to Lucy Dion and Judy Scott of the minister's office for their efforts on behalf of my constituents in Saint John-Lancaster.
Mr. Chairman, within the city of Saint John, New Brunswick, in the federal constituency of Saint John-Lancaster, there is a harbour. Within the Saint John harbour at the present time there is an anomaly called Rodney terminal. It is an anomaly because there is no other terminal owned and operated by the National Harbours Board which has been financed in such a peculiar manner. Though the wharf is owned and operated by the National Harbours Board, the Premier of New Brunswick agreed to guarantee the funding necessary. Presently, the province of New Brunswick has invested $20 million of provincial money, plus $5 million which the province borrowed from DREE in the form of a repayable loan. The National Harbours Board has invested $12 million which it received from Treasury Board in the form of repayable loan funds. In effect, we have the province coughing up $25 million and the owner and the operator, the National Harbours Board, contributing only $12 million into the project which has so far cost a total of $37 million.
Mr. Chairman, my question to the Minister of Transport is: Why should the province of New Brunswick have the only terminal in Canada owned and operated by a federal board but which is two-thirds funded by the people of the province?

Mr. Chairman, in response to this first question I must say that we have co-operated quite closely with the government of New Brunswick so that they could keep going; but they needed more help than we were able to give through the National Harbours Board. Now I can tell the hon. member, without citing any figure at the moment, that it is our intention to help more
May 13, 1975

if it is necessary. From what the hon. member is saying, it seems as though there is a necessity for there to be better co-operation from the federal authorities, and this is something we will do with pleasure.

Mr. Chairman, some time ago the minister told the House that the transportation policy now under study would embrace everything that moves and that it would be announced some time during the spring or summer. The minister further stated that the policy would cover not only regional air carriers but airports and highways. We have been waiting for the unfolding of this vitally needed transportation policy. I notice from reading the estimates that considerable funds are devoted to the function of strengthening the policy and planning programs of the department; I see a reference in the blue book, under these headings, to a sum of almost $19 million.
I rise to take part in the debate today following a brief reference by the minister last night to a change of direction with respect to air policy. His comments are to be found at page 5712 of Hansard. The change results from the fact that the regional carriers are now fully involved with the larger jets; the old policy was never designed to embrace this concept. To bring the matter into focus, may I remind hon. members that when the regional air policy was announced in 1966, the categories were reasonably flexible. The minister is aware of them:
(a)	Where appropriate, limited competition on mainline route segments of Air Canada or CPA may be permitted to regional carriers if this is consistent with their local route development.
(b)	In a few cases, secondary routes presently operated by Air Canada and CPA may become eligible for transfer to regional carriers.
(c)	A larger role will be allotted to regional carriers in connection with the development of domestic and international charger services, inclusive tours and new types of services.
It seems to me that those categories are still broad enough to embrace the advent of the jet plane. This view is supported by outstanding leaders in the field of regional air carrier service. Among them is the Hon. Lionel Chevri-er who is now president of QuebecAir. He criticized the application of the policy and accused Air Canada of an inexcusable lack of civic spirit in intervening before a foreign agency to limit the growth of Canadian regional air lines. I say this because before I reach the end of my remarks I want to get an opinion from the minister as to whether Air Canada is now moving back into some of the regional air categories it abandoned immediately before the announcement of the 1966 policy and thereafter.
Incidentally, that statement by Mr. Chevrier was reported in the Globe and Mail of February 13 of this year. More recently, on April 23, another leader in the regional aviation field, Mr. Arthur Mauro, of TransAir made very much the same point when he told the company's annual meeting that regional airlines were supposed to be granted additional passenger routes under the federal regional air policy announced in 1966, but that this had not happened. He suggested that the proper allocation of domestic routes would reduce the magnitude of the fare increases being requested by main line and regional carriers. Both types of carriers were losing money on short haul routes. Canada's route system should therefore be redesigned so that is would be more in keeping with the equipment and organizational structures of various carriers.
Business of Supply
This opinion seems to be reinforced by what the minister stated last night. We were given a preliminary idea of the upgraded policy by the minister's statement on November 23, 1973, which dealt with the international aspects of air policy. This was to be followed by an expansion of the regional concept affecting also the primary or third level carriers, as they are sometimes called.
I agree with the hon. member for Bruce-Grey who suggested that, if we are going to make these two essential parts of the air policy about to be enunciated serve the air transportation needs of Canada, we will have to use the hub and spoke principle. I think that is why the minister indicated that he is putting the emphasis on primary and third level carriers.
I bring the problem right into focus now in a specific area of Canada to which I have directed the minister's attention before. I refer to western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan, that area of Manitoba outside the city of Winnipeg which is in the southern part of the province. The minister has announced that there will be an experimental commuter service operating quite soon in co-operation with the province of Manitoba. I lay emphasis on the word "experimental" because this is to be a two-year experiment. It replaces a similar service that was being provided up to a year ago by Midwest, a subsidiary of TransAir. The reason Midwest asked for suspension of service a year ago was that it had to be subsidized. It was not economically viable. I understand that the proposed service is also going to be subsidized, and it will bring into air service communities like Brandon, Yorkton, Saskatoon, Dauphin, and so on. The point I want to make is that unless the hub and spoke principle is adopted, that service will not be any more useful than was the suspended Midwest service.
What is needed in this part of Canada is a jet service that will provide rapid access to the eastern market from these particular parts of southeastern Saskatchewan and southwestern Manitoba. I am sure the minister realizes this, because in an interjection last night he said: "They can make money by flying from Brandon to Toronto but not by flying from Brandon to Winnipeg". That is just the point I want to make. The hub and spoke principle, as enunciated by the hon. member for Bruce-Grey, demonstrates that you have to feed into these regional areas. In this particular part of Canada there would be a population of about 250,000 which would be a potential market for air services. Air service is urgently needed because the city of Brandon, for example, is the home of the provincial exhibition of Manitoba and of the Royal Manitoba Winter Fair, and it is becoming increasingly difficult to attract the interest of the eastern part of Canada, agronomists, and so on, in these fairs-which were, and still are outstanding shows on the continent-unless there is jet access.
The specific question I should like to ask the minister- perhaps he will also enlarge on some of the points he made in his preliminary statement last night-is this: Is it within the concept of the revised regional, air policy that is about to be enunciated that the commuter service necessary for gathering passengers from surrounding rural areas will be reinforced by a jet service that would operate out of Brandon airport? Air Canada flies over Brandon

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
about eight times a day in both an easterly and westerly direction. TransAir, the designated regional carrier, offered a jet service but this was turned down by an ATC decision. I trust the minister is taking a hard look at that decision to see whether the refusal is within his contemplated regional air policy and to see whether it is economically feasible. This was a service to be operated without a subsidy of any kind based on the availability of the new Fokker 28 jet aircraft.
I know that Air Canada has been asked by the province of Saskatchewan to review jet service to this area, and perhaps the minister can give us an insight into any decisions made in this regard. I am also aware that Air Canada is offering a jet service into Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, which is a community very similar in size to Brandon, though I doubt it will have a population base of some 250,000 upon which to draw.
In summary, this is a very urgently needed service. We encourage the minister to proceed expeditiously with his review. I feel the regional air policy can still fit pretty well within the original categories if sufficient flexibility is given to make use of the wide potential of the jet planes that are now available to all regional carriers.

Mr. Chairman, in regard to the policy of 1966 of switching air routes from Air Canada to the regional carriers, the hon. member made reference, not to Mr. Chevrier but to the other gentleman whose name I forget.
You mean Mr. Mauro of TransAir.

I can give the hon. member the list if he wants it, and he can ask Mr. Chevrier about it. Mr. Chevrier is with QuebecAir, one of the airlines that profits the most from routes which used to belong to Air Canada, one of which is Quebec-Bagotville-Seven Islands. I might point out that TransAir got the Thunder Bay to Toronto route, for example, in competition with Air Canada. So I think that kind of statement leads nowhere because there is no truth to it. If I am told it is insufficient, then we will discuss it further.
Be that as it may, we are now compelled by circumstances-this is something we will probably have to discuss shortly-to create a third level carrier. This is the experiment at Brandon, Yorkton, Dauphin and Saskatoon with the S-27, I think it is, manufactured by the government of Manitoba. The experiment has two purposes. First, it will give service to the area; second, it will be a good opportunity to test the aircraft to see whether it is suitable for this kind of service.
As far as jets are concerned, this is a matter for the ATC, as the hon. member mentioned. The ATC is a committee of the CTC, and it is the ATC that decides whether there is to be a service between two cities. Although there may be a change in the future, all I can say at the moment is that I am ready to discuss the matter with the CTC. But I am not sure that we are in agreement that it is a good thing to have new jets covering different sectors of the country so that one day we will be so overloaded by aircraft or by equipment that-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the minister, but the time allotted to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris has now expired.

Mr. Chairman, I was able to ask a few questions of the minister yesterday, and I listened carefully to most of the questions of hon. members yesterday and today, and to the minister's replies. Let me say at the outset that what I am about to say has nothing to do with my personal regard for the minister. I have a high personal regard for him and I hope that nothing I say from here on will be taken by him personally. I am sure he will not do that.
Earlier, in reply to the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville regarding Crowsnest pass freight rates, the minister said if there was going to be any decision, he would make it. Since the hon. member became Minister of Transport he has repeatedly made speeches in this House and has answered literally thousands of questions during the oral question period on various aspects of the whole transportation system in Canada and all modes. I should have thought by now he would have got the message that there needs to be some fundamental change.
He has repeatedly said the government will be coming up with a new policy. His predecessor, and the minister before him said the same thing. This sort of thing has gone on for some time in this parliament, and in the previous two parliaments: we have had a continuous litany of this sort of answer. I, for one, and I suspect most other members of this Chamber and the majority of the public in Canada, have run out of patience. We have heard great speeches, funny speeches, we have heard crying and whining by this Minister of Transport, and we have been asked to wait for this and to wait for that. I, for one, do not think we can wait any longer. We are tired of waiting. Our patience has been exhausted. It seems to me that three successive parliaments and the public generally have been more than patient, kind and understanding with the minister.
When this minister talks about making the decisions, whether they are in respect of Crowsnest pass rates or anything else, and says that he will be the one to do so, I should point out that we have seen nothing but a continual display of weakness and indecision. We have had no decisions from this Minister of Transport. When it comes to announcements or statements in respect of Crowsnest pass rates, who makes them? It is not the Minister of Transport; it is the Minister of Justice. When it comes to transportation studies in respect of grain movement in western Canada-and I would think that would be under the Department of Transport-who makes the announcement? I suggest the announcement is made by the Grains Council under the Minister of Justice.
When statements are made about branch line abandonments which are killing hundreds of communities in western Canada, who makes those statements? They are not made by the Minister of Transport; they usually come from the Minister of Justice.

Because he believes in capital punishment.
May 13, 1975

When there are speeches and statements to be made about rail line relocations, who makes them? They are made by the minister in charge of housing, or the Minister of Regional, Economic Expansion-but not by the Minister of Transport. When it comes to urban transit- and I should think that would have something to do with transportation-who makes the statements? Who made a speech in Toronto yesterday in this regard? It was made by the minister in charge of housing, not by the Minister of Transport. Who supported the railways in opposition to a CTC ruling on freight rates? Where was the Minister of Transport at that time? The Minister of Justice supported the case of the railways, not the Minister of Transport.
The railway company presidents, including the president of the one the people of Canada are supposed to own, have no compunction about making arbitrary decisions in respect of freight rates, totally ignoring the Minister of Transport. If one looks at the reply which appears at page 5640 of Hansard for last Friday, he will get an indication of how the railway companies ignore this Minister of Transport. The minister was asked a question by the hon. member for Mackenzie, to which he replied:
-I can say there is no law that says the railways must open their books. I tell you it is not being done. I asked for information last week and received a very nice answer saying that this is not going to be revealed to anybody, including the Minister of Transport. Someday I hope we will have an opportunity to discuss that here in the House.
I can remember one, two or three days of special debate going back to early 1969 when the same sort of thing was being discussed and the minister said something different. The presidents of these railroads can totally ignore the Minister of Transport; they act on the basis of being a law unto themselves. The president of the Canadian Pacific can rewrite history in respect of the Crowsnest pass rates or anything else. I am sure the Minister of Transport has had a few bitter experiences with that gentleman and that company.
The minister was complaining yesterday about there being so many Crown corporations that he does not know who they report to or how they report, whether through the department or through the minister to parliament. How many years has the hon. gentleman been the minister? He and his predecessors have had 12 years to bring in a new transportation policy. Where is this new policy? Where is this restructuring of transportation? Where is this fundamental change to our transportation policy and our transportation system in this country? This minister and his predecessors have sat idly by while our two railway systems have coldly and calculatedly, at the expense of the economy and the people of this country, allowed our railroads to deteriorate to a state where they are a national disgrace.
These companies have siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars for investment in shopping centres, high-rise office buildings, oil companies, pipeline companies and mining and processing plants while our railroads have been crying for help. As a result, we have totally inadequate and completely unfair freight and passenger services. We have a transportation system that discriminates against people of this country because of where they happen to live.
The minister has said that competition does not work in respect of transportation. Perhaps he limited that to rail-
Business of Supply
way transportation. I do not wish to misquote him or put words in his mouth. He said that two or three years ago. I am not suggesting things he does not already know; I am just reminding him of them. Where is the policy that will eliminate this discrimination resulting from a nineteenth century concept of transportation in Canada? Transportation services in Canada have deteriorated to the point where they are as bad as any in the world. No industrialized nation in the world still operates transportation on the concept of competition and profitability. Where is this fundamental change in transportation policy?
The complaints of members from all parties, and from members of the public in all parts of Canada surely should be sufficient to indicate to the minister that any policy he brings in will have to be fundamentally different. Such a policy must be so different that it will require courage, a massive effort and a great deal of leadership. Such a policy cannot be implemented by a Minister of Transport who allows himself to be undermined continually by his colleagues in the cabinet. It cannot be implemented by a minister who allows himself to be treated like dirt by the heads of the transportation companies in the country.
I hope when the minister uses the final 15 minutes tonight, and I intend to use my entire 15 minutes now, he will tell this parliament that he is either going to bring in that fundamentally changed transportation policy and stop all this fractionating that is going on in our transportation system, or he is going to quit. If he is not prepared to stand on his own hind legs and stop allowing himself to be pushed around and treated like some clown in the House of Commons-and we do not need any more funny speeches or jokes that get laughs from members of the press gallery-then we are not going to see this new transportation policy.
Mr. Chairman, the requirements of transportation and everything else in the economy depend on the integration of transportation. We keep messing around with concepts that were thrown out long ago by most countries. Transportation must be treated as a public utility, an essential public service. Yet the government seems still to think it can have a little bit of free enterprise here, a little bit of public enterprise there, a little bit of regulation here, a little bit of regulation there, a little bit of this and that, and a little bit of a Minister of Transport. This business will not work. You cannot have it both ways.
We might look at the countries of Europe, Japan and Australia. We must treat transportation as a public utility, owned and operated by the public and controlled by the public through the Minister of Transport, the government and parliament, with a utility rating board or whatever overseeing body might be set up. Instead of that, we keep enlarging the jungle and compounding all the inequities, discrimination and inadequacies of a transportation system. Nineteenth century concepts have got us into a mess here. Our railroad system across the country has failed year after year to meet the growth in the transportation needs of Canada. There is nothing new about there being a shortage of boxcars. I remember in 1946 and 1947 that there were not enough stock cars or refrigerator cars. That was forgiven because of the wartime period. They have never caught up. There has always been a shortage of

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
locomotives. I remember in the early 1950s when locomotives were leased from the United States.
The minister must, once and for all, say that the government will bring in a national transportation policy that will get rid of the concept of competition which cannot function in a public utility. It would be just as logical to have two competing highways running side by side, or two competing electrical or telephone companies. We did that years ago. It would be just as sensible to have two competing sewer and water systems running under our streets. This is nonsense. There have been duplications, inefficiencies, backhauls and failure to keep the system up to date. Some people in the government propose that perhaps we should take over the roadbeds of the railroads. They would love that. They have allowed them to deteriorate to a point where it will take something like $1 billion to put the roadbeds back into the standard they should be in. They have never kept them up. Where was the Minister of Transport-this one or his predecessor? Who was telling the railways that they had two choices, either compulsory or "you must"?
The same situation applies in respect of the airlines. The minister says that Air Canada is asked to do things for the country as a whole. I agree with his remarks about Air Canada yesterday. They lost $1 million on their Montreal to Moscow route last year. We asked Air Canada to do something we would not ask private enterprise to do. That has been the problem. The concept has been to siphon off the lucrative routes and pad up some regional carriers or CP Air to the detriment of our own airline. I am amazed that Air Canada has done as well as it has. Half a dozen of the largest privately owned airlines in the United States are presently on their hands and knees pleading with their federal authority for several hundred million dollars to bail them out. As I have said, I am amazed that Air Canada has done as well as it has. I submit it has done that despite the transportation policy of this government and despite some of the senior management. Had it not been for the quality and character of most of the employees, it would not have done as well as it has.
The way we handcuff our own airlines and railways is criminal. It is beyond belief. I thought that by now the minister, even if it means having a knock-down, dragged-out fight with some of his nineteenth century colleagues, would have said, "This will be the new policy, or I quit. This is what I want to bring to parliament. This is what we need to do about transportation." We have all this nonsense about flying DC-8 jets over 100-mile flights. It is ridiculous, wasteful and inefficient. One can get from downtown Ottawa to downtown Toronto more quickly on the turbo than on Air Canada. Try it. This is a waste. The CNR removed one passenger train when it got the turbo going between Montreal and Toronto, and something in the order of 10,000 or 15,000 automobiles a day go back and forth between Montreal and Toronto with one person in each car. Really, what is transportation policy? Why should people leave their automobiles behind? The congestion in our cities requires a massive effort on the part of the provincial and municipal authorities as part of our national transportation policy. We need an urban transportation system. It will take ten years and hundreds of millions of dollars to do it. It will also create tens of thousands of jobs.

The railroads refused to work together for the benefit of the various regions and areas of Canada. Why? They are supposed to be competing. The CNR and CPR have tracks side by side, but the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and some of his allies say that we must pick up branch lines way out on the prairies where farmers may have to drive an additional 15 or 20 miles to haul their grain. We have nonsense like that on the 45-miles between Regina and Moose Jaw. There are CNR tracks right beside the CPR tracks. You could remove those 45 miles of CNR track and nobody would be hurt. Then you would have a much more efficient and sensible operation between those two cities. But oh, no; they must compete.

speechtext: Order, please. The time allotted to the hon. member has expired.
I will be very brief, Mr. Chairman. I think the hon. member has not been very nice. He did not put any questions to me; rather, he made a series of attacks and I do not have an opportunity to answer.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I made it very clear to the minister that he would have 15 minutes tonight, and I hope he will do whatever he likes about what I said. There is no use asking questions any more. This has been going on for two years, and we get nowhere.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think it is worth while bringing to the attention of members that the Premier of Saskatchewan called an election today, and we are witnessing the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre conducting his campaign. It is interesting to note that he has the same backward-looking approach he has had for 20 years.

Mr. Chairman, I shall try to be a little nicer to the Minister of Transport. The port of Churchill is totally dependent on the CNR for the delivery of grain and other imported and exported materials to this great inland seaport. I have mentioned on other occasions in the House that this port is not used to its capacity, for the following reasons. First, there is lack of concern and effort by this government. This is reflected in the estimates we are discussing today. I feel that the money that is being spent on capital projects and also on maintenance projects represents nothing more than housekeeping. I do not feel this is good in relation to the expansion of the inland port of Churchill.
Most of the railway that runs from The Pas to Churchill has been upgraded over the last few years to the point where it is now capable of handling the hopper cars that have been built for the transportation of grain. However, the portion of the railroad from Gillam to Churchill has not been upgraded to this point. There have been several serious rail problems which have caused several wrecks. This has cost the CNR a large sum of money. It has also hampered the delivery of goods to the port of Churchill. Another problem between Gillam and Churchill which also affects the delivery of goods to Churchill is that there is no passing track from Gillam to Churchill, a distance of some 200 miles.
May 13, 1975

If the port of Churchill is to be brought up to its full capacity, we have to provide some money to upgrade the railway facilities and the facilities of the port itself. I would like to commend the members of the harbours board who deal with Churchill because the fellows I have met in Churchill who are working there are making a good, honest effort to upgrade this port facility, but we must have the help of the government in order to develop this port to its full capacity. I am not thinking now about submarines, and so on. I want the port brought up to the capacity of which it is capable.
The port at the present time is under the authority of the eastern region of Canada, which gives Montreal complete control over this very vital port. Why is this port not under the control of the western region where the goods shipped through that port originate? Grain comes from the central prairie region of Canada, sulphur is now coming from western Canada and is being shipped out through Churchill. Why is it controlled by the eastern region? Why can the control of that port not be in the hands of the western region where the people are closer to the situation?
Another problem with regard to the delivery of grain is the fact that there is no co-ordination whatsoever between the wheat board, the Department of Transport, and the harbours board. There does not seem to be co-operation in getting the grain to that facility and on to ships. I have stated before in the House that today when there are boats which can carry 1,300,000 bushels out of Churchill we must have better facilities and more storage capacity. Some of our trackage is completely plugged with the traditional type of boxcars, and that is why we have to upgrade our facility and the trackage in order to handle hopper cars, thus bringing the port of Churchill up to its full capacity with the facilities now there.
I was interested today to see the interest the harbours board is now taking in the diversion of the Churchill River. Hopefully not, but that will probably have some effect on the town of Churchill with regard to its water intake, and so on. I was pleased that the harbours board has the National Research Council carrying out a study.
I would also like to mention the air transport committee. In the area I represent we, fortunately or unfortunately, do not have Air Canada, but we have carriers like TransAir, Lambair, Calmair, Cross Lake Air Service, St. Andrews Air, Ilford-Riverton Airways and Parsons Airways. These carriers are not being subsidized to the tune of some $9 million. No one is picking up the tab for them. They must either provide a service and make it pay, or they are just out of business. When we consider the problems they have in making application for additional runs and reclassifying runs they already have, many of the air carriers, because of the time element and the slow rate at which ATC makes a decision, have to wait anywhere from 9 months to 18 months for a decision.
I say those air carriers are the backbone of transportation in the north at this time. At one time the railway was the backbone, but it has become such a dilapidated transportation system, and so undependable, that air transport is the key to transportation around the Churchill constituency, yet we are forcing these air carriers to violate the
Business of Supply
law almost every day because there has not been a decision handed down by the ATC.
The ATC should be considering the entire air carrier system. Perhaps we should be dealing with regions of Canada instead of trying to make rules applicable right across the country. There are air transportation problems which could be solved within each individual area. We also find that air carriers in many cases are not being considered for other regional contracts which come up, and I think they should be taken into consideration when these contracts are being let.
Freight rates in general are so out of line for people living in communities served only by the railway that it is at this point forcing not only small industry out of business in much of the Churchill constituency, but also some of the larger companies. I can cite International Nickel as an example. The Department of Transport appears to take the view that it can put a tariff on a particular item because the only way that item can be moved is by rail, but I can assure the minister that the companies are aware of this, and they feel they are being penalized. They are considering other means of transportation to move articles into their mine sites, and so on.
The small businesses along the railway to Churchill, and those along the railway to Lynn Lake are suffering an increase of 20 per cent. This was announced just last week in the area. It makes it impractical for small businesses to ship articles. That is not so for the large operator who can receive containerized goods, but the small operator is almost completely out of business because he does not have that alternative to move his goods. Many people in the smaller communities have begun chartering aircraft to move goods even though trains run right past their doorsteps because they can no longer afford to pay the rates set by the railway.
I would like to mention that the NTCL has moved into Churchill on a contract for the next 15 years to move goods up the coast of Hudson Bay. I welcome this type of development because this will help the port of Churchill. I hope this will be a jumping off spot for the development of the Arctic gas pipeline, which I hope will come down the west side of Hudson Bay. I can think of no better place than the port of Churchill as a distribution centre for that pipeline. The railway is there, ships have access, and so on. I think it would be a good move to get the facilities in shape now.
I see that there is also development on the airstrips at Eskimo Point, Whale Cove and Rankin Inlet. This is being done under the jurisdiction of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It will be very beneficial if the pipeline does come down the west side of Hudson Bay, where I think it should, because it is the only practical route.
I would like to ask the minister if he can give me any answer on the future development of the port of Churchill. Is the government just sitting back? Is the government completely controlled by the ports in the east? Why is Churchill not developed to its full potential of, say, 40 million bushels of grain per annum, as opposed to what the minister announced last year as another record year of 22 million bushels? I cannot accept that, when the facilities are already in place at Churchill and there are people

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
there who operate the port. I cannot understand why the port cannot operate to its full capacity.

Mr. Chairman, I have not got much time. I do not see why the hon. member draws a conclusion exactly opposite to that which he should draw. The port of Churchill had been very much neglected in the past and I have been negotiating with the government of Manitoba to change that. Before we met a year ago there was $12 million that we were supposed to spend in about six years. We decided to reduce the period to three years in order to expedite the project. Also, as the hon. member knows, we cannot use the port the year round and so we are trying to see how we can extend this period.
The hon. member asks why Churchill is serviced by ships or companies from Montreal. This year I decided that the company which is going to serve the North and the Keewatin area will be the NTCL. That is not a company from Montreal, and there have been complaints about that. It must be recognized that we are making an effort to pay $3.3 million for engineering purposes to see how we can develop the port of Churchill. This is at the same time that we are developing the port of Prince Rupert.
The emphasis could have been put on the port of Prince Rupert, but the government decided to do something for Churchill, and is doing it. The hon. member may say it is not doing enough. Mr. Chairman, we are dredging in the port of Churchill in order to allow ships to use the harbour more easily than in the past. We are not regressing, we are progressing. Maybe it is not fast enough and maybe next year we can go faster, but we have been worried about Churchill, as we have been worried also about Prince Rupert.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre forgot all this in his speech, because there was Prince Rupert, there was Churchill, and there was all the development we have done in the northern part of British Columbia. He did not mention the Clinton-Ashcroft bypass. This is of no interest to him. He did not talk about the strengthening of the highways so that trucking in the western provinces can move better than in the past. He did not talk about what we have done in the maritimes because he has no interest in that. But we have done something, Mr. Chairman, and there is something in the budget for Churchill. It is better than it used to be.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to take part in the debate because we are dealing with a very important problem in this country.
I am always astonished to realize how much Canada and ancient Greece are alike. In both countries the transportation problem was the one to solve to achieve national unity, economic prosperity at home and in our relations with our neighbours.
Mr. Chairman, because Canada has an area of four million square miles and 22 million people, as Greece is faced with a series of small communities which must be interconnected.

In my maiden speech, that was the problem to which I wanted to draw the attention of the House because it directly concerns people in my riding. Indeed, my constituents owe their very existence to the transportation system.
Before Confederation, of course, people used waterways, rivers and lakes to travel. Things have changed since and North Bay, as all the other towns in my riding, would not exist if the railway from this town towards the western coast had not been built.

Recently I had occasion to read a document called "Canada Courier", Volume 12, Number 9, which deals with the Canadian transportation industry. When Canada faces up to its transportation dilemma it will find solutions that will not only enhance communications between Canadians but which will also contribute to its future as a technological and industrial nation.
It is evident that since we developed our industrial power we have concentrated on transportation and a highly sophisticated transportation technology. I am reminded of the MLW controversy last year when we were attempting to export diesel engines to Cuba. We must realize that Canada is one of the main suppliers of diesel engines, and that is because of a highly developed technology in diesel construction. It was a surprise to me to find that Canada was one of the first developers of an international commercial jet airliner. Unfortunately the development was abandoned and Canada lost its technological advantage. That was followed by the abandonment of the CF-105, from which we still suffer.
We can look with pride on the government's involvement in the development of aircraft and air express technology. The "Canada Courier" referred to the DASH 7 and described it in glowing terms. When we see the DASH 7 coming out of the hangar we can take pride in it. As it was developed by de Havilland there was reason for the Canadian government to become directly involved in that company.
The situation in regard to the short takeoff and landing plane has been indicated by the hon. member for Bruce, and I believe the future of Canada resides in that particular domain. In the area I come from, short takeoff and landing planes have been serving the North Bay airport for some time and we expect the service to continue.
I should like to quote one paragraph from the front page of the "Canada Courier" relating to the aerospace industry as I think it describes succinctly what has taken place in that industry. The article reads:
Canada's aerospace industry manufactures a broad range of products, 75 per cent of which is exported to world markets.
In a country which is so very interested in export markets it is interesting to see that 75 per cent of the production of this industry goes to international markets.
The article continues:
Highly skilled technical and scientific personnel ensure the most advanced technology and production methods as well as the most meticulous quality control procedures. The results have been marked.
May 13, 1975

Production value in 1974 was approximately $700,000,000 of which almost $500,000,000 was exported.
We are talking about half a billion dollars' worth of exports.
The Canadian aerospace industry has produced first-class satellites like Anik, a communications satellite taking advantage of the most advanced space technology. I suggest that Canada can be considered as being among the world leaders in communications and transport technology.

If I may now deal with a question which is parochial in nature, so to speak, I would like to direct some questions to the minister whom I congratulate for his initiatives relating to the North Bay airport. Of course, it is not the most popular air terminal in the world. It is in fact a small air terminal which bears already the name of one of my predecessors in the House, Jack Garland. It had not formerly a large custom, but of late years it has been served by three air lines, including Air Canada which calls at the air terminal three times a day, Norantair, an air service of the province of Ontario for the North-East which calls four times a day, and another airline called Voyageur Bradley Air Services which calls regularly too.
So, the air terminal is serving about 400 people a day, and we feel now that the facilities leave much to be desired. There is no refreshments bar. The essentials are there, but it is not possible to have meals or refreshments there. Unfortunately too, the population of the area cannot be served by charter lines, because overseas-borne travelers must go through Toronto for customs clearance.
So, Mr. Chairman, Air Canada has in that building facilities that are, to say the least, shabby. I know that it is not directly due to the fact that this situation was brought to the minister's attention previously. All the representations I made to the minister until now have been successful. Of course, in that field, things change every six or seven months. I wanted to take this opportunity to call the minister's attention on the situation at that airport.
Needless to say that the facilities are inadequate, although the runway itself is one of the best in all northeastern Ontario, because it is where all the flights which cannot be directed towards Toronto, for one reason or another, because of a strike or bad weather, are sent.
So, we must often welcome great numbers of passengers of Air Canada or other international airlines which are forced to stop there. I would therefore ask the minister to give me some information or to indicate what he intends to do regarding that air terminal and its facilities.
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt, as I explained at the beginning of my remarks, that my region owes its very existence to the national transportation system. As I said, it is there that the transcontinental line originated from. [English]
Without doubt, the future of Nipissing, North Bay and Sturgeon Falls depends on transportation. Three railroads serve the area, the ONR, CPR and CNR.
Now that we are involved with the aerospace industry I hope the minister will remember the extent to which North Bay depends on the Department of Transport. The
Business of Supply
future development of the area is at stake. I therefore hope the minister will make sure that the area's facilities are adequate for present services and also for any contemplated growth in the future.

Mr. Chairman, first let me make a few comments about the STOL experiment. If the experimental service between Montreal and Ottawa proves to be a success, and if it is proven that the DASH 7 is really an aircraft with STOL performance, not only will some problems in Canada be solved but there will be industrial benefits as well.
About 15 days ago-this does not happen often-a French delegation came here because they were interested in the DASH 7. The head of the delegation was Mr. Ziegler, the man who conceived the Concord, that big supersonic aircraft. Incidentally I do not want to see it here. At any rate he is considered as the father of the Concord. The delegation he headed came here because it was interested in the DASH 7 and in the STOL system. Mr. Ziegler is the head of a company which is concerned about air travel between Paris and the Alps. He found that we have the kind of aircraft they need for their service in France. The delegation went to Toronto, to the de Havilland company, because they wanted to see the DASH 7.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman. I should like to answer the hon. member's second question after supper.

speechtext:
