At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The committee will again consider vote No. 1 of the Department of Transport.

Mr. Chairman, I note the minister is present and his officials are just arriving. I want to say, with no offence to the minister, because I am allowed 15 minutes, if I use the total 15 minutes I do not think that he has no answer to the problems I have chosen to bring before him this evening. However, I hope that he and his officials will consider them.
I was greatly alarmed last Friday when, during the question period, the minister stated he had received a letter from a railway company which said quite clearly that their books were their own, they were not going to make them available to anyone, and there was no law in this land that could force them to do so. That remark concerned me greatly. I understand the predicament the minister is in, Mr. Chairman.
Last evening I read the annual report of Air Canada. Having read a number of annual reports of a number of airlines in recent years, I was concerned about their annual report. I want to put my concerns on record, in essence broadcasting to the people of Air Canada the

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
questions I would like them to answer when they appear before the committee to defend that annual report.
For many months we have heard from the president of Air Canada that it is short-haul traffic that causes them trouble, and long-haul traffic that makes money. He said it is the short-haul traffic they have to look after that really costs them money. I saw no evidence of that in their annual report. They referred to the Rapido air service, but gave no special accounting. Does the Rapido air service make money for Air Canada? That is my first question. The reason I bring that to the attention of the minister and Air Canada is that this is a service only between Montreal and Toronto. They may have, and in fact should have, a separate accounting of that system.
Venturex Limited, a subsidiary of Air Canada, handles their charter service under two groups, CanPlan, and some other one. There is no special accounting and no amount estimated in the Air Canada annual report as to the profit or loss of Venturex. There is hardly any mention as to whether they lost money in their courtship with Wardair or whether they made an actual contribution toward War-dair's credibility to carry on, which I think they did, at a cost to Air Canada and the Air Canada structure generally.
The annual report says with regard to the STOL air operation that there is an "encouraging public response". The president of Air Canada complains about short-hauls costing them money, long-hauls making them money, the short-haul having to be subsidized by the long-haul, yet there is no report as to whether STOL air operations can become a money maker for Air Canada, only that there is an encouraging public response.
If I would like to make an examination of Air Canada's annual report as a shareholder of that company, and I must speak for several thousand shareholders in the constituency of Crowfoot, I would like to know whether the STOL air operation has the potential of being a money maker. If it has, is there any substance to the argument that short-hauls are costly for Air Canada?
I wonder about Air Jamaica and the operations there. Is that operation costing Air Canada money purely and simply because of a commitment to the foreign affairs policy of the government?
What about Canadair and the whole involvement of Air Canada in aircraft construction? Is that operation costing Air Canada money today? Will it eventually prove to be the noose around the neck of Air Canada, forcing it to accept aircraft manufactured by the Canadian aircraft manufacturing industry?
Most airline companies suggest, without a word of a doubt, how much of their income is derived from charter service. Air Canada's annual report does not suggest that at all. It just leads us to believe it is a functional operation, and a very worthwhile one.
Having made those remarks about our air policy, I now wish to deal briefly with our railroad policy. At page 21 of committee report No. 20 of the Standing Committee on Transport Communications, I asked Mr. Sinclair, the president of CP, the following question:
Do you believe that a transportation policy should be geared to region-
al interests, or for our international interests, or for our ability to compete internationally?
We are attempting to evolve a new transportation policy. I asked a very simple question, should it be geared to regional interests or international interests? I wonder what the minister's opinion is in that regard. Mr. Sinclair replied without any equivocation. His answer can be found at page 21 of the committee report. He said:
Quite frankly, Mr. Horner, I do not think transportation should be used as an instrument of regional equalization. I think there are more effective ways of bringing that about.
He left no doubt that transportation policies should be geared to our ability to compete internationally.
This brings me to the next subject with which I want to deal. I once debated in Regina the question of whether the Canadian Pacific Railway should be nationalized or not. I took the side that it should not be nationalized. I am not ashamed of that. I do not believe it should be nationalized. I am not ashamed of the present management of CP. I think they are good. Mr. Burbidge, Mr. Sinclair, Mr. Mar-tinelli are knowledgeable, capable men. However, from my vantage point I believe they are overlooking certain things and this evening I wish to draw a number of these omissions to the minister's attention.
As hon. members may be aware, there is a great publicity campaign currently going on across the prairies. The CP is spending thousands of dollars to convince the lowly farmers, or people they think of as lowly farmers, that there is a better way-and I know CP is not an easy aminal for the minister to get along with. In that same committee the question of grain shipments arose. The CP said "the bottleneck was on the prairies". That is a direct quotation. The minister in charge of western transportation-no offence to the present minister; I am aware of the fights that go on within the cabinet-came down hard and heavy on the side of the CPR. He turned out to be the spokesman for the CPR in Saskatchewan.
A few minutes ago I spoke about taking part in that debate in Regina. Well, I do not think the CP should be nationalized but I do believe it should perform a national service within the province of Saskatchewan. That is where the Minister of Justice and I disagree. On April 10, about a year ago, the Minister of Transport and I, at a transportation conference he called, sat and watched various spokesmen enlarge upon the ills of transportation.
The CP laid out a chart of a car cycle of grain car movements in western Canada. They said the total car cycle was 18 days. I have the chart before me, now. A car spent 1.7 days in the City of Calgary, 4.4 days moving from Calgary to Vancouver, and 4.4 days in Vancouver trying to get unloaded. So of the 18 days, it spent over half the time being made up into a big choo-choo train in Calgary, and going on being a big choo-choo train through the mountains, and trying to get that choo-choo train unloaded in Vancouver. So when the President of CPR tells the transportation committee that the bottleneck is really on the prairies, his own charts do not substantiate that statement.
He goes on to say, as we read at page 22 of the committee report that the whole cause is the five-day work week on
May 13, 1975

the elevators on the prairies. Mr. Chairman, the whole cause is not the five-day work week because, according to this same chart, the time the car spent on the prairies in spite of a five-day work week is 2.9 days; the car spent 2.9 days out of the 18 being loaded. So it is readily conceivable that the biggest bottleneck is Vancouver.
Has the Department of Transport investigated this bottleneck? Is it because of the inefficiency of the elevators? Should they work on what I ordinarily refer to as the spout and auger principle? Or is the bulk loading system preferable? Do these delays arise because loading facilities at Vancouver are based on a five-day week? These are questions which I ask the department to examine. If it has not done so already, I think it should. In any case it is important that the transportation committee of the House of Commons should consider these matters carefully.
I know from evidence given at the same committee hearings that between now and 1980 the CP plans to spend $30-40 million on the purchase of boxcars. Yet during the transportation conference the minister called on April 10, 1974, it was suggested that if they could cut the grain car cycle by one day the number of cars required could be decreased by 763. If they could lower the cycle by two days another 747 cars would be saved, making a total saving of 1,510. If they could cut that cycle by three days-these are CP figures I am quoting-they would save a further 754 cars.
Reducing the cycle from 18 days to 15 days is certainly not an impossible goal. With a reduction of three days, over 2,100 boxcars could be saved. This would save the Canadian government $40 million on the purchase of 2,000 boxcars. This gives some idea of what confounds me when I sit and watch an hour of slides being shown by CP on the basis of figures which cannot stand up to close, knowledgeable scrutiny. The CPR has been obsessed with the idea of breaking the Crowsnest pass rates. It has a disciple in the Minister of Justice. He, too, is obsessed with the idea of breaking the Crowsnest pass rates. I think other means could be found of providing efficient service to western Canada in the movement of grain.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to put a few questions to the minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) this evening. As was stated yesterday by my colleague the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), the estimates keep increasing every year, but services in our areas are constantly reduced. I have nothing against progress and updating. But if a service must be discontinued, we ask that it be replaced by a more adequate system, so that the people be better served. We should expect service commensurate with increased estimates, and better still in certain areas. Mr. Chairman, the minister is aware of air transport problems faced by the constituency of Villeneuve, and I would like to put a few questions to the minister concerning Val d'Or airport, which has had no radar for the past month and a half.
My first question is this: Since we are examining estimates, can the minister advise the House whether the estimates provide for the installation of new radar or
Business of Supply
similar facilities required for the smooth operation of air services at Val d'Or airport? And if so, can the minister tell whether this will be done soon? I raise the question because a number of air passengers in northwestern Quebec fear for their safety in foggy weather.

Mr. Chairman, I have answered this same question three times in this House over the past week, once for the benefit of the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) and another time for another member in the Abitibi area. Of course the forces left the airport with their equipment. We now have inspectors on site in order to determine what type of signal equipment is needed for maximum aircraft safety. As soon as I have their report, I shall be in a position to tell when we shall take action.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. My second question is this: Can the minister tell whether there were developments concerning another airport in the Northern part of my constituency of Villeneuve, the Chibougamau airport for which the people have been pleading for a number of years? It would serve an estimated population of 20,000. According to certain airlines a new airport in Chibougamau would be profitable. Can the minister tell whether there are developments on that matter?

Mr. Chairman, in the estimates, $2,700,000 are allocated to local or municipal airports. Of course, there is an order of priorities; we cannot build up airports everywhere. People tell me; "It seems it would be profitable. The hon. member should be able to go a little further than that with local authorities, which he probably knows quite well. I know some of them too. If he wants me to give him a hand, I can help him. He should be able to prove that the money would not be invested to allow one or two planes only to land."
There are already airports in the Lac St. Jean area; there is a very big one in the Saguenay area. That does not mean that there must not be one in Chibougamau, a city where there is industrial development. Besides, during the last elections, I went there and even visited a new barking plant of considerable importance. In any event, I think that a case must be made which will demonstrate that an airport is essential there. Then, we would be able to come to an agreement with the municipality and help them. However, I cannot tell him in such a candid way.
I remember a very simple incident which happened in my office when a full delegation told me: "We would like an airport at such a place". I answered: "What planes are going to land there?" They said: "Build up the runway and we shall see." Then, we should build up runways everywhere. All I ask you is that the case be made and, then, we will see how we can help.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday morning, I had conversations with the manager of Nor-dair, at Val d'Or, and he told me that he had submitted an application, I do not know whether it is to the minister or the Canadian Transport Commission, in order to get the privilege to go to Chibougamau to connect Val-d'Or and

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
Chibougamau; this is what makes me conclude that the company finds it profitable.

Mr. Chairman, Nordair might be interested because it is going to serve the whole area as it is already serving the Abitibi. The decision will be made by the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission. We shall see what their decision will be and if there are problems, we might discuss them.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister tell us if he is aware of representations made in order to discontinue the railway passenger service between La Reine and Senneterre?

As far as railway service between those two communities is concerned, as mentioned by the hon. member, I think it is under the jurisdiction of the CNR. I believe that the company needs the approval of the Canadian Transport Commission. I do not know whether the CNR has submitted an application to that effect, perhaps you might give me some more details as I do not locate those communities very well geographically. But, wherever they are located, the CTC must authorize the CNR to discontinue the service.

Mr. Chairman, I will try to be brief. I should like to discuss for a few moments some problems in the city of Calgary, but before doing so may I join in the remarks of the hon. member for Crowfoot with reference to Air Canada short-hauls. It is not so long ago that Air Canada had a route between Calgary and Edmonton. They claimed it cost them so much money that finally the route was given to a small branch company. The small branch company has made so much money that it is probably the gold mine of the west. So it sure boils down to straight management in these things.
In the city of Calgary we have the only airport in which the depot is owned by the municipality. In the days before we saw the new depots built at Toronto, Winnipeg and Edmonton-this was when the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings was minister-Calgary was missed, not because the government missed it intentionally but because the depot was owned by the municipality.
Then at the time Mr. Pickersgill was passing the bill through which he was going to become head of the Canadian Transport Commission, which ensured that he would get a good pension, the department negotiated a contract with the city of Calgary for the government to purchase the equity from the city. At that time it promised that within three years we would have a new depot. This was some time around 1966 or 1967. It is now 1975.
The old depot has been extended in all directions. During the winter it is equipped with electric heaters. Calgary airport is called an international airport, yet while you are waiting for Air Canada, if you happen to sit under one of the heaters you get one of those so-called Florida tans. Some say that they even interfere with the fertility of the human race, they are so hot. There are no decent washrooms. The ones they have are so dirty that even the hogs you find in rural areas in the northern part of Alberta would hesitate to use them.

There is no air conditioning at the airport, but there let me congratulate the minister. I once raised this matter in the House during an argument, and since then someone must have read about it and something was done. So I thank the minister for finally putting in some air conditioning to neutralize this terrific heat that you get when waiting for Air Canada in order to crowd on to a 747. They even have pens there. They must have thought they were in the stockyards.
We are now to have a $40 million shiny new depot for which we have waited ten long years. I sent a copy of a telegram I received to my good friend, the minister, who always tries to co-operate if possible within his own sphere of jurisdiction so as to deal with some of the monstrosities that exist in the Department of Transport. Some people claim there is a lot of hanky-panky going on with the tendering. Take, for example, a simple thing like tile. I should like to put this telegram on the record:
We request your intervention to rectify a situation that is very unfair. We are the low tender for the supply of Gail brickplate tile pavers, approved by the architects-
By the way, they are solid Grit too. I would have thought they were solid gold, but I do know they are solid Grit. They have never been known to go to anybody but the Grits, so they should be palatable to the government.
There are a few survivors?

There are a few survivors in Calgary, and that is what makes them such tremendous characters.
In any event, the title was approved and this company was the one which had its tender in on time. Then along came a company in the east, and my hon. friend laughs because it happens that the company is in her constituency. Apparently the officers of this company were great friends of another noble character in this House, who used to be the Minister of Finance and then the Minister of Transport. He was the man who could always predict the economy with such accuracy.
You mean Benson.

You guessed him; it was Benson. Apparently Mr. Benson at some time in his political career advanced a large sum of money to keep this company afloat. The company is still in some trouble and it wants to pull itself out at the expense of the Calgary company.
I have a telegram from Darlington Haskins and Company Limited of Vancouver, which is a branch of P. M. Dartnall Limited, Calgary. I might tell you that the man involved is a kind of character himself. I arrived here after seven hours on the plane-my wife had joined me on this trip-and at two o'clock in the morning he phoned me and he was in no humour to be soft-soaped in any way about this hanky-panky going on in respect of tenders for the Calgary airport.
I would ask the minister if he has an answer in respect of this matter, and I hope he does not tell me there is nothing wrong. I have done a little more research on this and I know that the tenders were closed. I think it was the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton who made a speech about the method of tendering on these contracts. An
May 13, 1975

election has just been called in Saskatchewan, and they say the only difference between the NDP and the Liberals is that the Liberals are full of money. I know they need money for their election, but I do not want it all to come from the Calgary airport and other projects in Calgary.
Seriously, I would like to hear what the minister has to say. Would he now promise to cut out this hanky-panky at our airport and please get it finished so that we do not lose our fertility in the city of Calgary just trying to catch Air Canada flights?

Mr. Chairman, I think the best way to answer these questions is to refer to a memo I received from Mr. Windsor who is in charge of airports in Canada. This is probably a confidential document but I am fully confident of my discretion. It states:
Following tender call by the Project Office for supply of quarry tile for Calgary terminal, it was brought to my attention that the specification was more stringent than the Canadian Government Specification Board Standard 75-GP-1B.
Subsequently, officials recommended that CGSB Specification was adequate for the purpose intended and inasmuch as there was insufficient time to issue an addendum to the tender prior to the close of tenders, the project office is now requesting quotations on the basis of the revised specification.
This was in reference to a tender call for floor tile for the Calgary airport.
Mr. Chairman, my sympathy is with the minister. The fact is that what has taken place was something over which he had no control.
Well, I thank you.

If I were the minister I am sure I would not have control, as he does not have control, over this hanky-panky stuff that goes on behind the scenes. Here we have an architect laying down the specifications, and then people come along and change them and a Canadian company loses the contract. This is a Canadian company, by the way, which employs about 1,500 people between Calgary and Vancouver. I know the Minister of National Revenue will appreciate that.
Because specifications are changed I hope the department does not tear up all the tenders. I do not blame the minister for this hanky-panky that is going on. I am going to sit down, Mr. Chairman, but I want to say that there is at stake some $40 million. I hope they do not tear up all the tenders and then grant these contracts on an ad hoc basis.
This is Calgary's centennial year. For 100 years we have been discriminated against in the city of Calgary, by taxation, and in the west generally by freight rates, and by having the poorest international airport in the world. Except for the character and the stamina of these people they would have gone under ground. However, we flourished as a metropolis, but we could still use the help of the minister to cut out this hanky-panky that is going on, or this little dealing under the table. We like to play poker on top of the table, but we have a feeling there is something going on under the table. I would ask the minister to take a look at the situation. Let us get this project built so that we can have some kind of equity and cleanliness.
Business of Supply
I think the only suggestion I can make at this moment is that, if I am still around when it happens, the hon. member is cordially invited to the opening of that new airport.
Let him cut the ribbon.
Let me thank the minister for his graciousness. Even if I have to stand on Grit tile, I appreciate the invitation.
This matter of tenders was discussed this afternoon with the Leader of the Opposition and other members, including the member for South Shore. Unfortunately he is not here.
I will take the message for him.

Yes, you take the message. I may be mistaken, but I think the Leader of the Opposition adopted exactly the same argument. He asked why we did not audit the books of the Harbour Commission in Hamilton in order to discover these things. If the hon. Leader of the Opposition did not use that argument I am sure the hon. member for South Shore did. As hon. members know, there are two commissions in Canada that operate under a special statute adopted by the House of Commons. They do not fall under the general rules, and the Hamilton Harbour Commission is one of the two. It states in that statute that the audit is to be made by the municipality and not by the federal government.
What about the bids?
The same thing for the bids.
I am talking about the St. Lawrence bids.
Oh, well, you changed the subject.
Oh, oh!
I understand you because, of course, you have no interest in the other one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the London District Railway Workers Council I should like to direct a few questions to the minister. That council stated in a letter to the minister that they have been informed by the news media that Mr. Bandeen, CN president, wants the CNR split into smaller companies as an economic shot in the arm, and the taxpayer as a shareholder would see his investment increase in value.
The Globe and Mail of April 5 also informed the council that the CN has sold the Chapman trucking firm on the west coast, wholly owned by the CNR, to a United States trucking firm. They suggest that this would be selling a part of a Canadian Crown corporation into foreign ownership. They point out that if Mr. Bandeen has this authority it would be logical to assume that he could sell off any part off the small companies into which he wants to split the CN.
It is interesting to note that on the CBC national news of Sunday, January 27, 1974, confirmed in the London Free Press of January 28 the same year, it was reported that the

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
trade minister and 33 Canadian businessmen attended a trade mission to Mexico, and that our government had agreed to a loan of $200 million for the purpose of upgrading their railways, while at the same time our own railways are being neglected and falling apart.
My question to the minister, to which I believe we are entitled to have answered, are as follows. First, were the four days of hearings held in southwestern Ontario by the Commons Standing Committee on Transportation from May 29 to June 1, 1972, mere tokenism? Second, if that is not the case, when does the minister intend to recommend the implementation of this committee report which was tabled in the House in June, 1972? Third, does the CNR president have the authority to split this Crown corporation into small subsidiary companies? Fourth, if the president does have that authority, does he have authority to sell these small subsidiary companies to private foreign-owned companies? Fifth, if the CNR is split up into small subsidiary companies what will happen to the employees and their bargaining units? Sixth, will they have a voice and be kept informed of proceedings? Seventh, did our federal government pay the $200,000,000 to Mexico?

Mr. Chairman, it is quite difficult to answer these questions outright. I think I will have to get in touch with Mr. Bandeen and discuss with my hon. friend the contents of this letter and the allegations contained in it, because I think this is a very important problem. Sometimes Crown corporations believe they can do almost anything. The government is interested in certain things the Crown corporations are doing. Maybe some of the Crown corporations even if the statutes do not compel them to do so, might inform the Minister of Transport of what they intend to do so that the newspaper men are not the first to know what is going on in certain Crown corporations. This is very serious.
If you will allow me to do so, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that the kind of debate which has been going on is something that personally I appreciate very much. It is very useful to have the points of view of everybody in respect of the real problems. It is frustrating for anyone who has an executive job to be in the situation of discussing something with the wrong facts. Probably this is true not only in respect of executives but also in respect of other jobs when the exact facts are not before one.
There was a reference in the House today to the third report on midwestern Ontario. Of course I do not remember all the reports that are filed and tabled here. I received the information later that this report had been tabled on May 1, 1974. I was asked what we did with this third report. I did not know offhand what we did with it. It was tabled on that date. I believe it is very important to check to find out exactly what is happening.
This is similar to the situation in respect of the hon. gentleman who was here a few moments ago and who is probably now behind the curtains, my good friend from Central Nova. He spoke of the vice-president of a personnel agency who opened a business, and suggested that Air Canada paid a fee of six months salary to this agency. Well, I looked into this and I did not find anything. If he has some evidence I think he should produce it to me so

that I can honestly look into it, but if it is only a rumour I think it is wrong.
If Air Canada does not behave as it should I believe it should be attacked, just like any other company. You never saw me attempt to protect any Crown corporation under my jurisdiction just because it was a Crown corporation. However, I do not think it is right to attack them wrongly. They do commit a number of sins but I do not think I want to react to all of them. We are often much more strict in respect of the Crown corporations than is the case in respect of private organizations. Some say no, but I am sure it is yes.
This afternoon the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre made a real effort to find out everything the Minister of Transport did not do and what other ministers did in the field of transportation. He forgot to mention all that has been done through the Ministry of Transport during the past year. Many things were done, not only in British Columbia as I mentioned. Twice this year in the west, in Ontario, in Quebec and in the Atlantic provinces I met with all the provincial ministers. I even met with some of the premiers in order to discuss the policy I intend to present first to the committee and then to the House. In my view this is very important if we are to have a coherent national policy.
I do not speak of a federal policy. I speak of a national transportation policy. If we want one I believe we must consult with the local people, the people in the regions, the cities and the provinces so that we will have a policy which really meets the need of the nation. We have been working hard. I am not speaking only of the trips I made and the discussions I had but also the discussions my officials and I had on a number of other problems.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And the opposition too.

And the opposition too. I know I am due to meet it in any event so I prefer to do it in a good atmosphere. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre forgot about all those things. He forgot about STOL and how important it is. He forgot about all the air agreements we have entered into in order to expand the air influence of Canada. He forgot about all we did in respect of the Northern Transportation Company and what we did in respect of the government of Manitoba. This is something on which we worked very hard. I worked with Mr. Evans and we succeeded in arriving at a formula. The hon. member did not talk about the highways and what we did in that field. He did not talk about the monitoring service which followed the meeting he had with me. He stated that that produced real results. He did not talk about the cost disclosure bill which came before this House.
It took three years.

It was passed this year. We had a nice agreement with the western ministers on the freight rates, and even the premier of Alberta said it was a really great breakthrough. The hon. member did not talk about the ferry service in the maritimes. He was not interested in that. Then there was the matter of protection of coastal trade and the adoption of the Darling Report. He was not interested in that. He was not interested in the
May 13, 1975

protection we gave to Canadian flag carriers. He did not talk about the development of the railroad in northern British Columbia or about the improvement at the airports of Calgary, Saskatoon, London and many other places. He was not interested in that. He did not talk about the improvement in safety standards. He was not interested in safety at the airports.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. Is the minister summing up his whole debate now?
No, just part of it.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question while he is summing up?
No. I am just answering Mr. Turner.
Which Mr. Turner?

I only wish to make the point that we should be reasonable. As we used to say, if you cannot stand the heat, get out of the kitchen. That is fair enough. I will talk in a few minutes about what we have done in the field of new policy, and after that, perhaps the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre will justify what he said when he started talking. He started by saying that he was not personally opposed to the Minister of Transport, but after that he criticized me all the time.
Mr. Chairman, it is good to see the minister in such a jovial mood tonight. I take it he was replying to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre.
No, no, it was a question by the hon. member for London East.

Mr. Chairman, I have a series of questions I would like to ask the minister, and a number of them arise from the debate which has been going on with respect to the Crowsnest pass freight rate. I take it there has been a change in the attitude or the mind of the minister from last October, because in the same exercise last October when we talked about the Crowsnest freight rate the minister indicated and implied that at that point in time no one in his department, and certainly no one in his office, was working on any changes with respect to the Crowsnest freight rate. Then on January 30, 1975, at page 2747 of Hansard in a question posed by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar the matter was again raised, and the minister replied that there had been no discussions or consideration with respect to changing any part of the Crowsnest freight rate. That was confirmed on January 31 in a reply to a question posed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert. The only thing the minister mentioned was the fact that he would not undertake to make that promise for the rest of the century.
In the discussion today it seems that the minister has implied that studies and consideration are going on with respect to the Crowsnest freight rate, and that in fact he is looking at means to transfer the advantage of the Crowsnest freight rate to the farmers of western Canada. I
Business of Supply
wonder if the minister could inform the House or elaborate on just what form that transfer might take and what sort of studies and consultations are taking place. I notice that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board is here, and he has indicated that he very much enjoyed the-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He is the associate minister of transport.

The hon. member for Peace River has said that he is the associate minister of transport. The Minister of Justice has indicated in a press release that he takes very seriously the input of western Canadian farmers, and I know that he has been out west discussing freight rates and the whole subject of rail transportation. I am wondering if the minister can take the House into his confidence and outline what kind of review there might be in respect of the Crowsnest freight rate, having regard to the fact that the subject of the Crowsnest freight rate is actively under consideration.
Will there be a change in the statutes? Will it be a form of subsidy to producers? Will it be in the form of a subsidy to the railway companies? I sincerely hope the minister will clarify that once and for all, because it is an issue which affects every western Canadian and particularly every western Canadian grain producer. If the minister could do that, I think the record would certainly be put straight, and hopefully that would allay the fears that the whole concept of the Crowsnest freight rate might be removed. But if the advantages are to be maintained, I think the minister owes it to this House and to the country to advise us of just what form the transfer of the advantage will take.

Mr. Chairman, once or twice this afternoon the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville put exactly the same question to me. The first time he was not satisfied with the answer, and I gave another answer. I do not know whether he is satisfied, but I have already given the answer. I would appreciate it if hon. members would read Hansard tomorrow. It is not that I do not want to make the effort of answering, but the more answers one gives, the more interpretations can be given to those answers. I prefer to maintain what I have already said.

Mr. Chairman, it is precisely this kind of thing which this committee is trying to clear up. The minister is now being as evasive as he was with the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville. If he cannot remember the answer, perhaps he might prevail upon his colleague, the Minister of Justice, to answer the question because he seems to answer these questions more frequently than the Minister of Transport himself. I listened very carefully to the response the minister gave to the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, and it was very cloudy and confusing.
I simply want clarification. If the Minister of Justice is prepared to stand in his place and respond, I would certainly accept his answer because I believe that the Minister of Justice has a plan and has been actively engaged in considering the Crowsnest freight rate, and ways and means to alter it. As the hon. member for Crowfoot pointed out in his contribution to this debate, we all know that the railways are engaged in a very vigourous campaign to undo the Crowsnest freight rate, and the minister seems to
5764

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
be acquiescing in their request. For example, we know, and I am sure that the minister knows, that the average per ton mile freight rate with respect to the Crowsnest pass is something in the order of 0.5 cents. The Chairman of the CPR in the transport committee the other day indicated that he considered a fair rate to be something in the order of four times that amount, yet at the same time we find that in moving grain from Thunder Bay to Montreal, which is not governed by the Crowsnest freight rate, CP Rail is charging 0.97 cents per ton mile.
If the minister is going to sit in his place and condone and acquiesce in that kind of action, to the destruction of the Crowsnest freight rate, aided and abetted by his colleague, the Minister of Justice, we in western Canada and we in this whole country are in for a rude awakening because this minister and the Minister of Justice seem to be on the road to ruining any advantages the transportation policy of this country may have for western grain producers.
I am not satisfied with the minister's answer, and I reiterate that if the Minister of Justice knows the position and the policy of the government better than the Minister of Transport, perhaps he may want to answer.

Mr. Chairman, these are my estimates and I am supposed to answer the questions. What I said this afternoon will appear in Hansard tomorrow, and it is not what the hon. member repeated. He can check Hansard to see what I said. All the freight rates are a part of the policy we are working on, and I stated that we will act in such a way that western farmers will not lose anything in the new transportation policy or the new freight rate structures.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the Minister of Transport how he proposes to transfer the advantage of the Crowsnest freight rates to the western Canadian farmer?
This is part of the general policy that we are going to discuss in a short time, Mr. Chairman, and I would be glad to receive any opinion that the hon. member may have.
May I ask the minister a further question, Mr. Chairman? Will legislation be introduced in the House at the appropriate time to deal with this aspect of the transportation policy?

I have every reason to believe that if the House agrees to discuss this in the standing committee-because it has to be referred to a standing committee of the House-then we will be in a position to discuss the new policy and the principles of what we intend to do before the end of June.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister would undertake to guarantee to the House that legislation will be brought forth before any changes are made unilaterally. Will the policy position papers that the minister is now improvising be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications to be dealt with as was promised by the minister on April 25, 1974, at

page 48 of issue No. 4 of the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications?
Mr. Chairman, there is one point I should like to have clarified. Which law is the hon. member referring to that should be modified?

I understand that the Crowsnest freight rates are statutory law. Will the minister undertake to bring forth legislation? We hear conflicting views. One time we hear the minister saying that the Crowsnest freight rates would not be touched; we hear the Minister of Justice saying that the Crowsnest freight rates would not be touched; and today we find that they will be touched and the advantages will be transferred. Will those advantages be transferred to the producers or will they be in the form of a subsidy to the railway companies?

Mr. Chairman, I am not in the position to say there will be any modification to that statute so I cannot guarantee that we are going to introduce legislation. It may very well happen that no legislation at all will be introduced on that subject.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister would undertake to tell the House what procedure the government is adopting with respect to the review of the Crowsnest freight rates? Is it going through the CTC? Is it going through the grains group? Is it going through the upper echelons of the minister's office, or is it being studied by the Department of Transport?

Mr. Chairman, as soon as the new policy on freight rates is discussed by the committee, or by the House, we may make some recommendations and those recommendations can be modified according to the suggestions of the opposition. I am not going to say at this time what is going to happen when the policy itself is still not defined.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Has the minister got authority under the National Transportation Act now to change the Crowsnest rates?
The hon. member can debate this at that time if he wants to do so.

Mr. Chairman, this commitment is like so many others that we have received from this minister. On February 24, 1975, and it was classified as a great breakthrough, we found in that report that there were changes with respect to rate groupings, changes with respect to maximum rate restrictions, long and short haul-I could quote ad infinitum the commitments that were made. In regard to the minister's commitment to establish rate groupings to aid industrial development in small centres which had been promised at that time, I wonder if the minister could now tell the House when these will be put in place?

According to the agreement we reached in the west recently, the railways are holding discussions with the provinces and trying to reach an agreement on this particular subject.
May 13, 1975

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret that I have to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Chairman, there are many questions that I should like to put to the minister about transportation in the Atlantic region-not the Crowsnest freight rates. Until we get a new policy, however, it seems that we are going to get just vague answers.
The minister said something this afternoon which I should like to have clarified. He referred to the changes in the Maritime Freight Rates Act raising the subsidy from 30 per cent to 50 per cent on goods moving outside the Atlantic region. That left the impression that we are doing very well. He did not mention the huge increase of 25 per cent, and likely more coming, on all movements within the Atlantic region, which will go hard with the small and middle sized business men in the area about which we are concerned. We welcome the raise to 50 per cent from 30 per cent for movements outside the Atlantic region, but we are more interested in stabilizing things within the region. That is one matter that I should like the minister to clear up for us.
I hope we will have some definite information on the new transportation policy that is coming out before the House adjourns for this session. I should like to ask the minister if there have been any requests from the province of Nova Scotia for special help for privately owned municipal bus companies in Cape Breton. These companies are writing to me and saying that, unless something special is done, they will go under. The situation is that grave, Mr. Chairman, and I could show the minister all kinds of correspondence about it. I realize this is primarily a provincial responsibility, but they do not seem to be handling it in Nova Scotia in a way to give some stability to the municipal bus companies.
I have a third question that I should like the minister to spend a few minutes on, and to be as specific as he can. I realize he cannot speak for cabinet, but when can we expect an announcement on whether his department is going to recommend a merchant marine for Canada? The minister has said on several occasions that he is in favour of this, and I have heard him refer to it myself. Is his department going to recommend this to cabinet and, if so, when can we expect an announcement? This is vital to the development of the Atlantic region, and I hope it will be in the new transportation policy.
I hope the minister will consider the movement of goods from the Atlantic region to central Canada and will look into the way in which the Maritime Freight Rates Act needs to be adjusted from time to time. How will the federal government, with the help of Atlantic province premiers, develop our superports so that we can take advantage of new technologies in transportation, deal more with the rest of the world by developing our export sector, and concern ourselves less with so-called internal transportation links between the Atlantic region and central Canadian provinces? These transportation links have been of concern to us for 100 years and we have made relatively little progress.
Business of Supply
I agree that in the metropolitan areas of the Atlantic region we have made substantial progress in the last ten years. This progress is not really the result of deliberate government policies but is the result of defence spending in Nova Scotia and growth of government services.
One million people, in Canadian terms but not world terms, are living on the margin of subsistence in the Atlantic region of this country. The government's policy must be geared to help them.
Let me repeat and clarify my previous questions, in case the minister has forgotten them. First, I wish the minister would clarify the statement he made today concerning the Maritime Freight Rates Act. It has been suggested that the act is of benefit to the Atlantic region. How will we continue to feel the benefit in the Atlantic region in view of the increase requested by the railways? Further, has the minister received requests from the government of Nova Scotia for special help for privately owned municipal bus companies in Cape Breton Island? These companies are constantly writing to me, saying they will go under unless something is done. Thirdly, when can we expect an announcement from the minister or the department saying that he or the department recommend the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine? I repeated my questions in case the minister forgot them.

Mr. Chairman, I said this afternoon that it is true, we improved the subsidy system of the Atlantic provinces. It is true that most rates were increased, although some have been decreased a little at our request, as we thought they were unjust. But we must consider this in terms of relationships, in terms of what has gone on in the rest of Canada. These increases did not take place only in the Maritimes; they took place everywhere in Canada. The subsidy which the Maritimes receive is something which they have and the others do not have. I think the hon. member was suggesting something like this, "You agreed to give us a 50 per cent subsidy on certain commodities, but it is not worth it, because rates have increased generally-
Who said it is not worth it?

That was the suggestion. The problem is this: the Maritimes, the Atlantic provinces in general, wanted to be in a position to compete in central Canada with their manufactured goods, and they received a subsidy of 50 per cent on a great number of commodities. The fact that there was a 25 per cent, 20 per cent or 15 per cent increase across the board in Canada does not change the relative position of the Maritimes. That area has received a special subsidy because it is located far from markets. This statement holds true for the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act and for the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
I think we provided about $22 million to the Atlantic provinces under the assitance legislation, and $14 million under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. It is unjust not to mention that, and to say, "But you must not consider that, because our rates have been increased." I say that you were not placed in an unfavourable position on account of these increased freight rates. Of course you do not like it. I do not like it. I do not like inflation, and I do not like price
29561-2U/2

May 13, 1975
Business of Supply
increases. Neither does anybody else. In Europe, the United States and elsewhere, people do not like these things. As I say, we do not like it, but your relative position is better than it was. We have reached an agreement. I met with the hon. member's provincial minister. I even met with the premier of Nova Scotia.
Even with the premier?

Oh, yes! I have no prejudices! We said on that occasion, and I think this was published in the newspapers, that if any industries in the Atlantic provinces are affected by these increases, which are being asked for by the railways, to the point where they must curtail their production or close down, please communicate with us and we will see that such industries are given special help by the CTC or the federal government. Up to now we have received no demands, or no requests at all, only complaints in general terms like the one made a few minutes ago. I do not think we can establish a meaningful freight structure in Canada that way.
We have worked on the policy all year and we are convinced, more than ever, that we must deal separately with each region. The problem is not the same everywhere. The problem of northern Ontario is not that of southern Ontario; the problem of the Atlantic provinces is not that of B.C.; the problem of the prairies is not the problem of parts of Quebec.
And it took you five years to find that out? We have heard that so often from you.
Yes, you have heard it.
From you.
Yes, from me.
Well, do something.
We want to do something, not only talk about it.
Your speech has not changed in the last two years.
And your questions have not changed one iota.
And you still insist on making that same speech.
Not only are the questions the same, but-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman-
-most of the questions are in the same category. Up to 95 per cent of the questions which have been asked today in committee are questions-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the minister's zeal for transport policy in Canada, but I wonder if he can answer the second and third questions I asked.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Perhaps I should remind hon. members that, according to the agreement already accepted by the committee, the minister is speaking during the last 15 minutes allocated to him in order to summarize all points which were brought to his attention. At 9.30 a member of the official opposition will be entitled to speak for 15 minutes and close the debate.

Mr. Chairman, I tried to be as cool as I could; but some always find a way to provoke me. I can take it and shoot back, to be sure, particularly after hearing the kind of questions I have heard here for two days. We were discussing transportation in Canada and trying to find a new policy which will bring more justice, more equality to the transport system of Canada, and all we have heard are small and mean questions concerning one small corner of Canada.
You call freight rates a small item? Nonsense! This is something we shall remember.
Those are the kinds of questions which were asked 95 per cent of the time. The other 5 per cent was taken up with cries of a kind which have nothing to do with argument, reason or intelligence.
We shall see just how small an item freight rates are.

Most members, I know, are convinced that transportation is a serious matter. Some say that I keep repeating the same thing. Of course I do and I am going to keep on repeating it, because I want something to be understood very well by all Canadians and by the majority of this House.
We have to take into account the special conditions of each region so that the policy we develop is equitable, accessible and efficient. We do not want a transportation policy such as that set out in the old act where it must first be economic, then efficient, and then adequate. This is something which has some bearing in the law. We have been working on it. We have not been working alone, but with the provinces and the railways.
Answer his questions. The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond did not put mean questions. He is not getting answers.

The Leader of the Opposition does not understand the rules of the game. At this time I have 15 minutes to sum up and close this part of the debate. Following my remarks, a member of the opposition will be in the same position. Therefore I do not have to answer any more than I have done. The Leader of the Opposition is just trying to take a few minutes away from me.
Oh, oh!

speechtext:

Business of Supply
Canada. I thought there was a good cross-section of views put forward in the past two days.

speechtext: Order. I have been listening to the hon. member, and I think he should make a strong effort to address himself to the Chair.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I apologise. Any further remarks to the minister will be made through yourself.
We have all heard the term "too little and too late". I always hesitate to use it because it is a stock phrase to use when speaking as a member of the opposition about a minister or a government department. Nevertheless I think it perfectly describes the situation which now exist-it describes the efforts of the minister and his department to rectify the situation which has developed over the past few years. One can go over the policy guidelines which the government has used for the last two election campaigns and see that virtually no part of that program has been implemented. The minister has finally got a larger staff; we have seen a substantial increase, a 39 per cent increase in the staff of the department itself. It seems the minister is finally beginning to realize the extent of problems with which he is faced.
As to the ambivalent statements respecting the Crows-nest pass rates and the jurisdictions of the two ministers, the Minister of Transport and the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, I venture to say that the Minister of Transport is not quite sure of his ground in connection with the Crowsnest rates. I should like to pass on a word of caution to the Minister of Transport. If there is any attempt to change the Crowsnest pass rates without legislation there will not only be a rebellion in the House of Commons, there will be a rebellion throughout western Canada. I would point out that there are two studies going on at the present time, one is the Snavely study in which a costing account will be done-it will take about eight months-and the other is the Hall Commission which will take about 18 months. I say to the minister, and to the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, that it would be foolish to bring in any change whatsoever regardless of the new policy we are

talking about as far as the Crowsnest pass rates are concerned.
Once again, and I am not speaking politically, we in the official opposition sincerely believe the Minister of Transport is not giving any direction to his department. He is not giving any leadership. I commend the deputy minister for sitting through this debate. Possibly the most important aspect of the whole debate is that we feel the Minister of Transport does not understand the importance of transportation in such regions of the country as western Canada, the maritimes, and northern Canada. This has been demonstrated time and time again. If the minister can convince the official opposition that he is making an effort to change his attitude we shall certainly give him all due credit.
I had intended to mention the unfulfilled promises contained in the transportation policy which the Liberals presented in 1974-promises which have not been fulfilled. I shall not do so because my time is running out. The fact is that very few of these promises have been implemented in any way at all. When the minister reacts with irritation to criticism from this side of the House that he is not doing anything, we are entitled to bear in mind the failure to carry out the policy put forward at the time of the election and draw our own conclusions.

We will have the new modes of transportation policy that the minister talked about some time in June also before the transportation committee. All that is left for me to say at the present time is that this kind of debate has been constructive. I think it has brought the problems of transportation in various areas of the country to what you might consider front and centre stage. In doing that hopefully it will focus the attention of the minister and his department on the various problems which were raised and alluded to over the past two days.
I conclude by saying that we on this side of the House certainly welcome any move or policy commitments in the upcoming months, and we will take part to the fullest extent in any policy debate on transportation in the future.

Mr. Speaker, this matter is so serious that I expect to give the members on the government side far more time than I take to answer these accusations. I put it to the House, through you, Mr. Speaker, that the present position is shocking and intolerable. It is a grievance that must be brought up in the House. We have a situation where the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by what is the equivalent of a Papal Bull, is saying that a civil servant cannot appear before a committee The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) appeared before a committee of the House and
Public Service
said that civil servants can only appear when he allows them to appear, that they can only say what he allows them to say.
I suggest to the members of the House that it is this House that is the highest court in the land, and that we cannot tolerate any decision that exempts a minister or a civil servant from the rules that apply to all others. If a witness is called before a committee and refuses to appear or to answer, then he or she can be committed for contempt. Why then should civil servants be exempt?
I recognize that there are situations when civil servants should not be allowed to answer questions. The secretary to the Privy Council, or the secretary to the Cabinet, should not be allowed to answer questions dealing with what went on in Cabinet. Of course, I do not think an awful lot goes on when we see the results. Nevertheless, he should not be allowed to answer questions as to what goes on in Cabinet. Outside of that he is no better than anybody else in this country, and if he is called as a witness he should be compelled to appear.
I know my hon. friend is going to talk about responsible government. Of course we have responsible government, or we used to have, but the government is not very responsible now. Responsible government does not mean that civil servants can be exempted, or that they are above the law and should not be competent and compellable witnesses. That is what I would like to hear my hon. friend speak on when he replies.

IMMIGRATION-VIETNAMESE REFUGEES-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON REQUESTS BY OTHER COUNTRIES THAT CANADA ADMIT CERTAIN NUMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to obtain a reply to the supplementary question I posed on May 1 asking whether the Canadian government has approached, or will be approaching the new government of South Viet Nam with a request to allow relatives of Canadian Vietnamese to immigrate to Canada. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) referred this question to his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen).
My supplementary question was prompted by disturbing press reports about the chaotic circumstances surrounding the abrupt withdrawal of Canadian diplomatic personnel from Saigon on April 24, 1975, five days before the official surrender of the Government of South Viet Nam to the P.R.G. As a result, more than 3,500 sponsored or nominated relatives of Canadian residents were stranded in South Viet Nam. I hope that they are not abandoned.
Canada has an enviable record of humanitarianism. Our country has assisted in many ways in the reunification of thousands of families. Since 1946, 10 per cent of all immigrants to Canada have been refugees. This humanitarian tradition is the pride of Canadians, and a credit to Canada's enlightened and courageous governments.
This same humanitarian tradition must be carried on by our government by assisting sponsored and nominated Vietnamese relatives of Canadian residents. Canadian immigration officials sent over 3,500 letters to heads of families in Viet Nam promising Canadian visas. These people and their relatives in Canada are awaiting our government's action to help reunify their families. Canadians have a pride in their country's reputation for diplomatic excellence, and our government should not spare any effort, any peaceful avenue, to make known to the new government of South Viet-nam that we would like the stranded relatives of Canadian Vietnamese to be allowed to emigrate to Canada.
Furthermore, it has been reported that there are more than 30 Canadians in South Viet Nam, including some missionaries and their families. Their status is unclear. Their safety may be in danger. That is why I ask what the Canadian government is doing to assist these unfortunate people.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have an opportunity to respond to the question put by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz). His concern for humanitarian considerations, his concern for immigrants, and the special interest he has
Adjournment Debate
taken in immigrants to this country, both in his own constituency and in the country at large, are well known.
With regard to the question he has raised concerning the families and relatives of the Vietnamese people, the government is now considering the question of recognizing the new government in South Viet Nam and establishing diplomatic relations with that country. If diplomatic relations are established and a Canadian mission is sent to Saigon, the question of relatives of Canadian citizens being allowed to come to Canada would be a natural subject for discussion in view of the government's well known policy of encouraging the reunification of families of Canadian citizens.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-NURSES IN HALIFAX-REQUEST FOR CONSIDERATION OF WAGE PARITY IN VIEW OF POSSIBLE STRIKE
PUBLIC SERVICE-NURSES IN HALIFAX-REQUEST FOR CONSIDERATION OF WAGE PARITY IN VIEW OF POSSIBLE STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I live in a part of Halifax which is a block away from the Camp Hill Veterans Hospital. This is an ancient structure not in the style of the modern hospitals. Fortunately it is to be replaced soon. If one goes over there, as I do about 20 times a year, one will find that the veterans are complaining about a good number of things, but I believe this is in the tradition of veterans. The one thing they have never complained about is the quality of the nursing services they have received from the dedicated women whose case I wish to bring before the House this evening.
I have been there and I have seen men, in the last stages of going out of this world, surrounded by these angels of mercy. These are scenes I find impossible to describe in this House, but which will be written on my heart and my mind until the end of my days. Therefore I have no hesitation, and indeed I have a great deal of willingness to enter into the battle on behalf of these people. I feel that their pay position is bad, and I hope that sometime I will be able to tug sufficiently at the strings on the heart of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) in order to correct it.
For years the Conservative candidates in Atlantic Canada have stood for the removal of these iniquitous regional inequities, and in the last election campaign we were joined by our friends from the other side. Liberal candidates meeting in Halifax expressed their support for a full examination of existing regional wage policies to ensure greater equity for all within the federal public service. This included such senior adornments as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), plus the more junior ministers, the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc), and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald).
There were 32 Liberal candidates who took those words forth on the hustings in the last federal election and, given the circumstances of that election, this immediately became translated into removal of regional wage discrimination and inequity. But we now know that those were very hollow words indeed because only recently the nurses at Camp Hill Hospital, and other nurses, continued their fight to remove these inequities by making public protests, one day strikes and the like.

May 13, 1975
Adjournment Debate
It is a fact that in 1964 there were about 25,000 in the federal government employment staff who received regional rates, and in 1974 under the "just society" this number was 48,300, almost twice as many. The actual increase was from 15.5 per cent of strength to 19.5 per cent of strength. I provide these figures thanks to my colleague, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forre-stall), who has pursued this with the help of a member of his staff named Henry Brown with remarkable vigour and strength of purpose.
It is no wonder then that Halifax nurses at Camp Hill Hospital and nurses in other parts of Canada can complain, but in the case of Halifax their complaint is not only that the nurses there are not receiving the average for federal nurses across Canada, they are not even achieving what is paid to provincial nurses, and yet the President of the Treasury Board, the present incumbent in that position, in writing my colleague on March 4 said that:
The Treasury Board, as the employer, seeks to pay public servants rates of pay comparable to those paid by other employers for similar occupations.
That is simply hogwash as it concerns the nurses at Camp Hill Hospital. On May 1, 1974, I wrote to the then president of the treasury board, the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury), and I quote:
Dear Mr. Minister:
Two wards at Camp Hill Hospital are now closed because of a shortage of nurses. Surely this cries for a whole new approach to a federal policy which is driving nurses away from the employ of the federal government.
Nothing has happened to alleviate that particular situation. The number of wards occupied at Camp Hill Hospital is still down, and there are still vacant wards, vacant beds and vacant space, at a time when veterans are growing older and when there is obviously more of a cry for medical attention for them. If this does not tear at the conscience of hon. members, I do not know what can.
Finally, a doctor from Halifax who is a very respected member of the medical community, has written me about the salary policy of the federal government, and I quote:
When they come down east, the game has a new set of rules. The principle now is to pay regional pay rates, and not a consistent rate across the country. Thus they can pay federally employed nurses at Camp Hill Hospital the relatively low regional rates, rather than the much higher salary scales paid to federally employed nurses in Ontario. Paying federal employees on regional pay scales seems a clear principle as well.
But how come the rules change according to the circumstances?
He writes more than that, but that is the question I pose in winding up these remarks. My argument is not only to overcome the disparity that exists between nurses federally employed in the Halifax area and their sisters in provincial employ, but also between these federally employed nurses and their sisters employed elsewhere in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-NURSES IN HALIFAX-REQUEST FOR CONSIDERATION OF WAGE PARITY IN VIEW OF POSSIBLE STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to respond to the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). His concern for his contituents in that area is commendable. The pay policy is a regional one, that is, people employed in one area of the country will be

paid rates comparable to rates in the private sector and other wages in the area.
The pay proposal of the Treasury Board for the majority of nurses in the Halifax area represented 26.1 per cent in the first year and 12.7 per cent in the second, retroactive to December 30, 1974, with considerable improvements in vacations, which in fact provides not only comparability but parity with nurses employed by the provincial governments.
This, as part of the total Treasury Board offer, was seen to be "fair and reasonable" as a basis for comparability by all three members of a recent conciliation board, including the nurse's own representative, the president of Quebec Nurses Inc. This unanimous conciliation board report has been accepted by the Treasury Board but has not yet been sent to the nurses for ratification by the professional institute.

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-TOLLS ON RIDEAU-TRENT-SEVERN WATERWAY-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH CORTS COMMITTEE BEFORE IMPOSITION
NATIONAL PARKS-TOLLS ON RIDEAU-TRENT-SEVERN WATERWAY-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH CORTS COMMITTEE BEFORE IMPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) follows on one asked by the hon. member for Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack) concerning the authorization of the first ever tolls on the Rideau-Trent-Severn waterway.
I am particularly disturbed about this toll on a waterway that was used first of all for military purposes, then for commerce and trade, and goes through the heartland of Ontario connecting Lake Huron and Georgian Bay with Lake Ontario. It travels for a couple of hundred miles through some of the most scenic and agricultural country in the world. There are two very fine lift locks which people come hundreds of miles to see, and the waterway serves a population of over 60 million people.
I think this is a very backward step on the part of the minister. At one time there were tolls on the roads in Ontario-the last one at Bradford about 40 miles north of Toronto. At one time it was used for oxen and horses and carts, but the toll was abolished because the province began to build highways into the north country to develop it. The main waterway we had then was the one which connected Lake Ontario to Georgian Bay and went from Trenton along Lake Ontario to the Ottawa River, down to the St. Lawrence. This is a particularly historic area and I am amazed that the minister would impose this toll without consulting parliament or consulting the CORTS Advisory Committee which was appointed by the province to work in conjunction with the federal government.
I suggest that at no time has the CORTS Advisory Committee advised the imposition of tolls. Rather, it boasts of the fact that here was an area which people could enjoy, an area rich in history. And it has a great history. Hon. members who know their history will recall that Champlain came to Georgian Bay, and established the first white man's agricultural land on the north American continent. We look with pride on our history; we look on this land with a sense of history, knowing it was used by Indians before Champlain came there. Yes, Champlain himself stopped over in that area of the country I have the
May 13, 1975

honour to represent. It seems sacrilegious for someone now to come along and say that we must impose tolls on the canal. The tolls are for what? We are proud of this area. This land is part of Huronia. The settlers who came to the area built up Canada. Now those who want to use the waterway are to be taxed.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-TOLLS ON RIDEAU-TRENT-SEVERN WATERWAY-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH CORTS COMMITTEE BEFORE IMPOSITION
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-TOLLS ON RIDEAU-TRENT-SEVERN WATERWAY-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH CORTS COMMITTEE BEFORE IMPOSITION
speechtext:
I regret that the minister did not see fit to consult the CORTS Advisory Committee, and ask it what it thought was the best thing to do. After all, the committee did not meet all that long ago. I think that you, Mr. Speaker, were a member of this House when Mr. Pickers-gill said in this House that this area is a great tourist attraction and has brought the province a great deal of money. Many people are attracted to the area. He suggested that Uncle Leslie, that great premier of Ontario who has since gone to his reward and who won the respect of Liberals, Conservatives and NDP members, should be given a suitable birthday present. He was to be asked to carry on the tradition of this province in a suitable and honourable way. This was not done.
Previously, action was taken under the Conservative government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). That government, in its wisdom, set aside $20 million for the repairing of the Rideau-Trent-Severn waterway. Two locks were to be put in. Let me be fair to those members of the Liberal party who acted on this matter. Hon. George Mcllraith, now a member of the other place, looked at plans concerning the waterway system and told me personally that what was proposed was good, that the plan was good, and that so far as he was concerned as minister, the plans would be carried out. I go further and say that the plans were carried out to the letter. Now a minister without sense of history has come along and is doing things differently. Perhaps he does not know the history of the area as perhaps you, I, and others in Ontario and Quebec know it. Perhaps he has lost perspective, has forgotten history. I suggest that those who forget the past can never deal with the future.
The government has already taxed the voters of the area in connection with certain changes which have been made. Now the minister is proposing another tax, a toll to be levied on those who use the waterway. I remind that House that people have built cottages along the waterway. They rented the land from the Department of Transport and paid taxes on it. Incidentally, the rent was recently increased. Those people experienced difficulties in carting the lumber to the area. They hewed down trees of the forest in order to build their houses. Now, if they want to
Adjournment Debate
use their cottages and they have no roadway in, they must pay a toll. In my opinion this is deception. I am a bit disturbed and a little disappointed that the minister has put on this tax.
In conclusion I want to ask some questions. What is the minister going to make out of this? What amount of money is he going to collect on it? What is he going to pay for the services he is giving? Where is that money to be spent? Is it to be spent on the Trent Canal, or not? The minister has not given any satisfactory answer to those questions.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-TOLLS ON RIDEAU-TRENT-SEVERN WATERWAY-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH CORTS COMMITTEE BEFORE IMPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his comments. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) raised the matter of the relatively recently constituted CORTS Advisory Committee not having been consulted by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) in the matter of fees being charged on the Rideau-Trent-Severn waterway.
The CORTS Advisory Committee is a body of ten private citizens, five appointed federally and five provincially, to advise the federal and provincial ministers of the public response to programs and developments in the canal corridor. Treasury Board had approved the increase in Parks Canada user fees for national parks, national historic parks and sites and canals on February 4, 1975. The CORTS Advisory Committee was created by the signing of the CORTS Agreement on February 20, 1975. Therefore consultation was impossible. The fees which Parks Canada is charging are not limited to the canals, but apply throughout the program. They are based on the recovery of a portion of the annual costs resulting from a major capital investment program of $376 million during the next five years. In the case of canals, the cost recovery is estimated to be 7 per cent of the annual operating costs of the canals.
It would be incongruous for the government to apply new or increased levels of fees for national parks and sites throughout Canada while leaving the canal's activity free from similar charges. It is a modest return on investment made by and for Canadians. The money is to be used to improve the system and to preserve the history of which the hon. member speaks so eloquently.
